Chess in C and Silicon

A chess engine in C, then in silicon

Made by swr06

Write a small chess engine in plain C. Rebuild the same engine as SystemVerilog hardware. Prove the two agree on every move, run it on the PYNQ-Z2's programmable logic, and finish with a game you play from a serial terminal, drawn on a VGA monitor by your own GPU.

Blue steps: C on the CPU Green steps: RTL on the FPGA Amber steps: Vivado and the board Purple steps: the playable game

0Before you start

This guide builds one thing twice. First you write a chess engine in about 550 lines of C, small enough to read in an evening. Then you build the same engine again as a circuit, and prove, move by move and node by node, that the hardware gives exactly the same answers as the C.

The work is split the way the Zynq is built:

The programmable logic does the thinking: given a position, it searches for the best move. The Cortex-A9 does everything else: it reads your moves from the UART, checks them, keeps the game's history, and draws the board through your GPU library.

Sending the whole board for every search sounds wasteful, but it is the right design. A position is only 26 register writes, and the search that follows visits about a million positions. It also makes the system robust: the CPU always holds the true game, so nothing can drift out of step.

How each step works

Every step follows the same rhythm, in both halves of the guide:

  1. Concept. What problem this step solves, explained with pictures you can play with.
  2. Code. A short snippet. Each snippet's header tells you which file it goes in, and whether it starts the file (Create) or goes on the end of it (Add to). Copy the snippets in order and you will have the complete project.
  3. Check. How to prove the step is right before moving on.

The interactive figures run a JavaScript copy of the C engine inside this page. That copy was tested against the C engine on every test vector, so what the figures show is exactly what your code will do.

Part 1

The engine, in plain C

The C engine has two jobs. It teaches each algorithm in a form you can run in seconds, and it is the golden model: the reference that the hardware must match exactly. Everything lives in one header, c/chess.h, which any program can include.

1Squares and bitboards

Goal: describe a chess position with nothing but numbers, in a form that both C and hardware handle well.

Concept

Give every square a number from 0 to 63. Start at a1, go along the rank to h1, then up to the next rank:

square = 8 × (rank − 1) + file   (file a = 0 ... h = 7)

So a1 = 0, e1 = 4, e4 = 28, a8 = 56 and h8 = 63. Hover over the board to see how any square gets its number.

Now the key idea of this whole project. A 64-bit number has exactly one bit per square. So we can store "where are the white pawns?" as one number, called a bitboard, where bit n is 1 if a white pawn stands on square n. At the start, the white pawns are on squares 8 to 15, so their bitboard is 0x000000000000FF00.

Twelve bitboards hold every piece on the board: six piece types for each of two colors. The index is color × 6 + type:

Index01234567891011
PiecesPNBRQKpnbrqk

Three more facts finish a position: whose turn it is, which castling rights are left (four bits: white kingside, white queenside, black kingside, black queenside), and the en-passant square, if a pawn has just moved two squares. We use 64 to mean "no en-passant square".

The move word

A move fits in 15 bits: six for the from-square, six for the to-square, three for a promotion piece.

BitsMeaninge2 to e4a7 to a8, promote to queen
5:0from square1248
11:6to square2856
14:12promotion: 0 none, 1 knight, 2 bishop, 3 rook, 4 queen04
as a number0x070C0x4E30

There is no "capture" flag and no "castling" flag. The position already tells you if something stands on the destination, or if a king moved two squares. Fewer fields means fewer ways for the C and hardware to disagree. And since a1-to-a1 can never be a real move, the move word 0 means "no move".

One small trick: promotion codes 1 to 4 equal the piece-type numbers of knight to queen. So the promoted piece's board index needs no conversion at all.

Code

This first snippet starts chess.h: the types, the position, and macros to build and take apart move words. MAKE_MOVE(12, 28, 0) is e2 to e4.

Create c/chess.hpart 1 of 18
/* chess.h - the whole golden chess engine, in plain C (C99).
 * Include it from any program: #include "chess.h"                     */
#ifndef CHESS_H
#define CHESS_H

#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>

typedef uint64_t U64;     /* a bitboard: bit n is square n (a1 = 0, h8 = 63) */
typedef uint16_t Move;    /* bits 5:0 from, 11:6 to, 14:12 promotion        */

enum { WHITE = 0, BLACK = 1 };
enum { PAWN, KNIGHT, BISHOP, ROOK, QUEEN, KING };   /* piece types 0..5 */
enum { WK = 1, WQ = 2, BK = 4, BQ = 8 };            /* castling rights  */

#define NO_EP     64      /* "there is no en-passant square"       */
#define MAX_PLY   32      /* deepest search, same as the RTL stack */
#define MAX_MOVES 256     /* room for one move list                */

/* One chess position. The board index is color * 6 + type,
 * so bb[0] is the white pawns and bb[11] is the black king. */
typedef struct {
    U64 bb[12];
    int side;      /* WHITE or BLACK: whose turn it is            */
    int castle;    /* castling rights still available (WK|WQ|...) */
    int ep;        /* en-passant target square, or NO_EP          */
} Position;

/* Squares and move words */
#define BIT(sq)                    ((U64)1 << (sq))
#define MAKE_MOVE(from, to, promo) ((Move)((from) | ((to) << 6) | ((promo) << 12)))
#define MOVE_FROM(m)               ((m) & 63)
#define MOVE_TO(m)                 (((m) >> 6) & 63)
#define MOVE_PROMO(m)              (((m) >> 12) & 7)

Notice that Position holds no "occupied squares" bitboard. We calculate that when we need it, so it can never go stale.

Line by line

  • #ifndef CHESS_H ... #define CHESS_H is an include guard: if two files both include chess.h, the second copy is skipped, so nothing is defined twice.
  • typedef uint64_t U64: one bitboard. Bit n is square n, where n = rank × 8 + file, counting from 0. So a1 is 0, h1 is 7, a2 is 8, e4 is 3 × 8 + 4 = 28, and h8 is 63.
  • typedef uint16_t Move: a move packed into 15 bits. e2e4 is from 12, to 28, no promotion: 12 + 28 × 64 = 1804, or 0x070C. Packing a move into one small number makes move lists cheap to store, and in Part 2 a move fits in one 15-bit RAM word.
  • enum { WHITE = 0, BLACK = 1 }: because the colours are 0 and 1, !side is the other colour, and side * 6 is where that colour's boards start.
  • The piece-type enum gives PAWN = 0 up to KING = 5. The promotion field reuses it: 1 to 4 are knight to queen, and 0 means "no promotion".
  • Castling rights are four separate bits, so they combine with | and test with &: "White can still castle short" is castle & WK.
  • NO_EP is 64, one past the last square, so it can never be confused with a real square. MAX_PLY 32 is the deepest the search may go; the hardware stack in Part 2 has exactly 32 rows. MAX_MOVES 256 is comfortably above the most legal moves any chess position has (218).
  • Position: twelve boards, indexed color * 6 + type. The black knights are board 1 × 6 + 1 = 7.
  • BIT(sq) casts to U64 before shifting. 1 << 40 would shift a 32-bit int and is undefined behaviour in C; (U64)1 << 40 is correct.
  • MOVE_FROM, MOVE_TO and MOVE_PROMO undo MAKE_MOVE: shift the field down to bit 0, then mask it with 63 (six bits) or 7 (three bits).

2Bit tricks

Goal: learn the four operations that answer almost every question about bitboards.

Concept

With bitboards, questions about sets of squares become single operations on numbers:

ExpressionMeaningChess example
a & bin bothsquares I attack that hold an enemy piece
a | bin eitherall my bishops and queens
~anot inempty squares, from the occupied ones
a << 8move every bit up one rankwhite pawn pushes

Two more are less obvious and worth working through once, because loops over pieces use them constantly. Take b = 0110 1000 in binary:

Expected output
b           = 0110 1000
b - 1       = 0110 0111     borrowing flips the lowest 1, and every 0 below it
b & (b - 1) = 0110 0000     the lowest 1 is gone

-b = ~b + 1 = 1001 1000     two's complement
b & -b      = 0000 1000     only the lowest 1 is left

So b & (b - 1) removes the lowest piece, and b & -b isolates it. A loop over every piece in a set looks like this:

C
while (pieces) {
    int sq = lsb(pieces);       /* the lowest square in the set */
    /* ... use sq ... */
    pieces &= pieces - 1;       /* remove it; the loop ends when the set is empty */
}
Code

The masks are named sets of squares: FILE_A is the a-file, NOT_A is everything else. lsb finds the number of the lowest set square, and count_bits counts the set squares. Processors have instructions for both, and GCC and Clang expose them as __builtin_ctzll (count trailing zeros) and __builtin_popcountll; on the Cortex-A9 they become two instructions. The #if keeps a plain loop as a fallback for other compilers, so the file still builds anywhere. This one change makes perft about 30% faster. side_pieces combines one side's six boards, and occupied combines both sides.

Add to c/chess.hpart 2 of 18
#define ALL_SQ   (~(U64)0)
#define FILE_A   0x0101010101010101ULL
#define FILE_B   (FILE_A << 1)
#define FILE_G   (FILE_A << 6)
#define FILE_H   (FILE_A << 7)
#define NOT_A    (~FILE_A)
#define NOT_H    (~FILE_H)
#define NOT_AB   (~(FILE_A | FILE_B))
#define NOT_GH   (~(FILE_G | FILE_H))
#define RANK_1   0x00000000000000FFULL
#define RANK_4   0x00000000FF000000ULL
#define RANK_5   0x000000FF00000000ULL
#define RANK_8   0xFF00000000000000ULL

/* Number of the lowest set square. b must not be 0.
 * GCC and Clang (including Vitis's ARM gcc) turn the builtin into one or two
 * instructions; the loop is a portable fallback for other compilers. */
static inline int lsb(U64 b) {
#if defined(__GNUC__) || defined(__clang__)
    return __builtin_ctzll(b);
#else
    int sq = 0;
    while (!(b & 1)) { b >>= 1; sq++; }
    return sq;
#endif
}

static inline int count_bits(U64 b) {
#if defined(__GNUC__) || defined(__clang__)
    return __builtin_popcountll(b);
#else
    int n = 0;
    while (b) { b &= b - 1; n++; }      /* each pass removes one bit */
    return n;
#endif
}

static inline U64 side_pieces(const Position *p, int color) {
    const U64 *b = p->bb + color * 6;
    return b[0] | b[1] | b[2] | b[3] | b[4] | b[5];
}

static inline U64 occupied(const Position *p) {
    return side_pieces(p, WHITE) | side_pieces(p, BLACK);
}

Every function here is static inline. That lets the whole engine live in one header: each program that includes it gets its own copy, and the compiler does not warn about functions a program does not use.

Line by line

  • FILE_A is 0x0101010101010101: one set bit in each byte, and each byte is one rank, so it is the bottom-left bit of every rank, the a-file. Shifting it left by one gives the b-file, and so on.
  • NOT_A, NOT_H, NOT_AB, NOT_GH exist to stop wrap-around. Moving a set one square east is b << 1, but a piece on h4 (bit 31) then lands on bit 32, which is a5: it has wrapped onto the next rank. Every square east of a piece is never on the a-file, so (b << 1) & NOT_A removes exactly the wrapped bits. Moves two files east use NOT_AB.
  • RANK_4 and RANK_5 are where a double pawn push lands for White and Black. RANK_1 and RANK_8 are the promotion ranks.
  • lsb(b) counts the zero bits below the lowest 1. For b = binary 10100 it returns 2. It is undefined for 0, so every caller checks b first.
  • side_pieces ORs one colour's six boards together; occupied ORs both colours. Both are a handful of instructions, which is why the position does not store them.

One idiom appears in almost every function from here on. It visits every square in a set, lowest first:

C
while (b) {                 /* until no squares are left       */
    int sq = lsb(b);        /* the lowest one                  */
    b &= b - 1;             /* remove it: 10100 & 10011 = 10000 */
    /* ... use sq ... */
}

Subtracting 1 turns the lowest 1 into 0 and every 0 below it into 1, so the AND clears exactly that one bit.

3Knights, kings and pawns

Goal: for any set of knights, kings or pawns, find every square they attack, in a handful of operations.

Concept

An attack is not the same as a legal move. A pawn attacks diagonally even when nothing stands there, and a pinned piece still attacks. Attacks are the basic building block for both "is the king in check?" and "where can this piece go?".

Shifting a bitboard moves every piece at once by the same number of squares. A knight on square s can jump to s + 17, + 15, + 10, + 6, − 6, − 10, − 15 and − 17. So the knight's attacks are just eight shifts ORed together.

Shifts know nothing about the edge of the board, though. A knight on h4 (square 31), shifted by + 10, lands on square 41: b6. That is not a knight move. It wrapped around the edge. The fix is a mask: a knight that moves two files to the right can never land on file a or b, so we throw those squares away.

StepShiftMask after shifting
Up a rank+8none needed: it falls off the top
Down a rank−8none needed
Right+1NOT_A
Left−1NOT_H
Up-right, down-right+9, −7NOT_A
Up-left, down-left+7, −9NOT_H
Knight, two files right+10, −6NOT_AB
Knight, two files left+6, −10NOT_GH

Because the functions take a set, the same code works for one piece or for all of them. Pass all your knights and you get every square any of them attacks. That is what makes the next steps so short.

Code
Add to c/chess.hpart 3 of 18
/* Shift every bit by s squares: up for s > 0, down for s < 0. */
static inline U64 shift(U64 b, int s) {
    return s >= 0 ? b << s : b >> -s;
}

static inline U64 knight_attacks(U64 set) {
    return (shift(set, 17) & NOT_A)  | (shift(set, 15) & NOT_H)
         | (shift(set, 10) & NOT_AB) | (shift(set, 6)  & NOT_GH)
         | (shift(set, -6) & NOT_AB) | (shift(set, -10) & NOT_GH)
         | (shift(set, -15) & NOT_A) | (shift(set, -17) & NOT_H);
}

static inline U64 king_attacks(U64 set) {
    return shift(set, 8) | shift(set, -8)
         | (shift(set, 1) & NOT_A)  | (shift(set, -1) & NOT_H)
         | (shift(set, 9) & NOT_A)  | (shift(set, 7)  & NOT_H)
         | (shift(set, -7) & NOT_A) | (shift(set, -9) & NOT_H);
}

static inline U64 pawn_attacks(int color, U64 set) {
    if (color == WHITE) return (shift(set, 9) & NOT_A)  | (shift(set, 7) & NOT_H);
    else                return (shift(set, -7) & NOT_A) | (shift(set, -9) & NOT_H);
}

White pawns attack up and to the sides (+9 and +7). Black pawns attack down (−7 and −9). The king is the eight single steps.

Line by line

  • shift(b, s) exists because C cannot shift by a negative amount. Positive s moves pieces up the board (towards rank 8), negative s moves them down. Bits pushed past bit 63 or below bit 0 simply disappear, so the top and bottom edges of the board need no masks at all. Only the left and right edges can wrap.
  • A knight jump is one of eight offsets. Up two ranks is +16, so up two and right one is +17, up two and left one is +15. Up one and right two is +8 + 2 = +10, up one and left two is +6. The other four are the same jumps downwards.
  • Each offset that moves right must not land on the files it cannot reach: one file right can never land on the a-file (NOT_A), two files right never on a or b (NOT_AB). Moves to the left use NOT_H and NOT_GH.
  • knight_attacks takes a set, not one square. Pass it all your knights at once and you get every square any of them attacks: one call instead of a loop. The attack map in Step 5 depends on that.
  • The king's eight steps are ±8 (straight up or down: never wraps, no mask), ±1 (sideways) and ±7, ±9 (diagonal).
  • pawn_attacks covers captures only. Pushes are not attacks (a pawn cannot capture straight ahead), so they are generated separately in Step 8.

4Sliding pieces

Goal: rooks, bishops and queens: slide along a line until something is in the way.

Concept

A rook moves along a ray until it hits a piece. The square it hits counts as attacked, because whatever stands there might be capturable (or, if it is your own piece, defended). Squares beyond it are not attacked.

So we walk the ray one square at a time. The set set holds the front of the ray. Each pass steps it one square, adds the new square to the attacks, and then drops any ray that has just hit a piece:

The loop handles any number of sliders at once: if set holds both rooks, both rays advance together. A bishop is four diagonal rays, a rook is four straight rays, and a queen is both.

Notice the blocker's square is attacked, even when it is your own piece. We remove our own pieces later, in move generation. Keeping them in the attack set means the same function can say "my pawn on d6 is defended".

Code
Add to c/chess.hpart 4 of 18
/* All squares reached by sliding from every piece in "set" in one
 * direction (s = step, mask = squares a wrapped step can never reach). */
static inline U64 slide(U64 set, U64 occ, int s, U64 mask) {
    U64 attacks = 0;
    while (set) {
        set = shift(set, s) & mask;   /* step one square              */
        attacks |= set;               /* this square is attacked      */
        set &= ~occ;                  /* only empty squares go on     */
    }
    return attacks;
}

static inline U64 bishop_attacks(U64 set, U64 occ) {
    return slide(set, occ, 9, NOT_A)  | slide(set, occ, 7, NOT_H)
         | slide(set, occ, -7, NOT_A) | slide(set, occ, -9, NOT_H);
}

static inline U64 rook_attacks(U64 set, U64 occ) {
    return slide(set, occ, 8, ALL_SQ) | slide(set, occ, -8, ALL_SQ)
         | slide(set, occ, 1, NOT_A)  | slide(set, occ, -1, NOT_H);
}

The while loop runs at most seven times per direction, because a ray can cross at most seven squares. Hold on to that fact: in Part 2 it is the reason this loop turns into just three layers of logic.

Line by line, with an example

Take a rook on d4 with a pawn on d6, and slide north (s = +8). set starts as just d4.

  1. Pass 1: shift moves the set to d5. d5 joins attacks. d5 is empty, so it stays in set.
  2. Pass 2: the set moves to d6, and d6 joins attacks: the rook attacks the blocker (that is how captures happen). d6 is occupied, so set &= ~occ removes it, and the set is now empty.
  3. The loop ends. attacks is {d5, d6}: everything up to and including the first piece.
  • The blocker may be one of your own pieces. It is still included: the square is "defended". Step 8 removes your own pieces when it turns attacks into moves.
  • mask plays the same role as in the knight: east-going directions (+9, +1, −7) use NOT_A, west-going ones (+7, −1, −9) use NOT_H, and straight up or down needs no mask (ALL_SQ).
  • Because set may hold several pieces, one call slides all of them at once. bishop_attacks and rook_attacks just combine four directions each, and a queen is simply passed to both.

5The attack map, and check

Goal: one function that answers every "is this square attacked?" question in the engine.

Concept

Since every attack function takes a set, we can compute everything one side attacks with five calls: pawns, knights, king, then bishops and queens together (both slide diagonally), then rooks and queens together. The result is the side's attack map.

"Am I in check?" is then a single AND: is my king's bit inside the opponent's attack map?

Code
Add to c/chess.hpart 5 of 18
/* Every square attacked by every piece of one color. */
static inline U64 side_attacks(const Position *p, int color) {
    const U64 *b = p->bb + color * 6;
    U64 occ = occupied(p);
    return pawn_attacks(color, b[PAWN])
         | knight_attacks(b[KNIGHT])
         | king_attacks(b[KING])
         | bishop_attacks(b[BISHOP] | b[QUEEN], occ)
         | rook_attacks(b[ROOK] | b[QUEEN], occ);
}

/* Is the side to move in check? */
static inline int in_check(const Position *p) {
    U64 my_king = p->bb[p->side * 6 + KING];
    return (side_attacks(p, !p->side) & my_king) != 0;
}

This map does a lot of work later. It decides whether a move left your king in check, whether castling crosses an attacked square, and in Part 2 the hardware computes it in a single clock cycle.

Line by line

  • b points at the six boards of one colour, so b[KNIGHT] is that colour's knights.
  • occ includes both colours: any piece stops a ray.
  • Queens are added to both the bishop set and the rook set, because a queen moves like both.
  • in_check asks one question of the map: is my king on a square the other side attacks? !p->side is the opponent.

Computing the whole map to answer one question looks wasteful, and a CPU engine would instead look outward from the king. We keep the simple version on purpose: it is short, obviously correct, and it is exactly what the hardware builds, so the C and the RTL can be compared line for line.

6Making a move

Goal: play a move on a position, including captures, en passant, castling and promotion.

Concept

Engines search by trying a move, looking deeper, then taking it back. "Taking it back" is a common source of bugs, so we avoid it entirely with copy-make: copy the position, then change the copy. The parent is never touched, so there is nothing to undo.

C
Position child = *p;            /* copy  (a Position is 112 bytes)   */
make_move(&child, m);           /* make  (p itself is unchanged)     */

The hardware does the same thing: it keeps the parent on a stack and builds the child in a separate register. So copy-make keeps the C and the RTL close.

make_move does six things, in order:

  1. Capture. Clear the destination square on all six enemy boards. No flag is needed: if nothing is there, nothing changes.
  2. En passant. If a pawn lands on the en-passant square, remove the enemy pawn behind it.
  3. Move the piece. Clear from, set to. For a promotion, set to on the new piece's board instead.
  4. Castling rook. If the king moved two squares, move the rook too.
  5. Castling rights. Anything leaving or arriving on e1, a1, h1, e8, a8 or h8 removes the matching rights. This one rule covers a king moving, a rook moving, and a rook being captured.
  6. New en-passant square. A double pawn push sets it to the square it jumped over. Every other move clears it.

The rook squares for castling come from two small formulas:

Expected output
e1 to g1:  rook_from = to + 1 = 7 (h1)     rook_to = (from + to) / 2 = 5 (f1)
e1 to c1:  rook_from = to - 2 = 0 (a1)     rook_to = (from + to) / 2 = 3 (d1)
Code
Add to c/chess.hpart 6 of 18
/* Castling rights lost when a piece leaves or lands on square sq. */
static inline int rights_lost(int sq) {
    switch (sq) {
    case 4:  return WK | WQ;     /* e1: white king */
    case 7:  return WK;          /* h1 rook        */
    case 0:  return WQ;          /* a1 rook        */
    case 60: return BK | BQ;     /* e8: black king */
    case 63: return BK;          /* h8 rook        */
    case 56: return BQ;          /* a8 rook        */
    default: return 0;
    }
}

/* Play move m on *p. Callers copy the position first ("copy-make"). */
static inline void make_move(Position *p, Move m) {
    int us = p->side;
    int from = MOVE_FROM(m), to = MOVE_TO(m), promo = MOVE_PROMO(m);
    U64 from_bit = BIT(from), to_bit = BIT(to);
    U64 *mine   = p->bb + us * 6;
    U64 *theirs = p->bb + (!us) * 6;
    int moved = PAWN, t;

    while (moved < KING && !(mine[moved] & from_bit)) moved++;

    /* 1. Capture: clear the destination on all enemy boards. */
    for (t = PAWN; t <= KING; t++) theirs[t] &= ~to_bit;

    /* 2. En passant: the captured pawn stands behind the destination. */
    if (moved == PAWN && to == p->ep)
        theirs[PAWN] &= ~(us == WHITE ? to_bit >> 8 : to_bit << 8);

    /* 3. Move the piece. Promotion codes 1..4 equal KNIGHT..QUEEN. */
    mine[moved] &= ~from_bit;
    mine[promo ? promo : moved] |= to_bit;

    /* 4. Castling: the king moved two squares, so move the rook too. */
    if (moved == KING && (to == from + 2 || to == from - 2)) {
        int rook_from = to > from ? to + 1 : to - 2;
        int rook_to   = (from + to) / 2;
        mine[ROOK] = (mine[ROOK] & ~BIT(rook_from)) | BIT(rook_to);
    }

    /* 5. Castling rights. */
    p->castle &= ~(rights_lost(from) | rights_lost(to));

    /* 6. En-passant square: only right after a double pawn push. */
    if (moved == PAWN && (to == from + 16 || to == from - 16))
        p->ep = (from + to) / 2;
    else
        p->ep = NO_EP;

    p->side = !us;
}

The first line finds which of our six piece types stands on the from-square. A switch statement, rights_lost, lists the six special squares, so step 5 is a single line.

Line by line, following the numbered comments

  • Which piece moves? The while loop tries our pawns, then knights, and so on, until it finds the board with a piece on from. It stops before KING, because if no other board matched, the piece must be the king.
  • 1. Capture. Rather than find out which enemy piece stands on to, it clears to on all six enemy boards. Five of the six operations change nothing, but there is no branch and no search, and the result is always right.
  • 2. En passant. If a pawn moves to the en-passant square, the pawn it captures is not on to but one rank behind it: 8 squares lower for White (to_bit >> 8), 8 higher for Black.
  • 3. Move the piece. Clear from on the mover's board, then set to. On a promotion, the bit is set on the new piece's board instead: promo is 1 to 4, which are exactly KNIGHT to QUEEN.
  • 4. Castling is the only move that moves two pieces. The king moved two squares, so the rook jumps over it. For e1g1 (4 to 6): the rook comes from to + 1 = 7, h1, and goes to (4 + 6) / 2 = 5, f1. For e1c1 (4 to 2): from to − 2 = 0, a1, to (4 + 2) / 2 = 3, d1. The same formulas work for Black, 56 squares higher.
  • 5. Castling rights. Any move from or to e1, a1 or h1 (or their black twins) loses the matching rights, whether the king or rook moved or a rook was captured. rights_lost returns the bits to clear.
  • 6. En-passant square. Only a double pawn push creates one: the square it passed over, (from + to) / 2. For e2e4 that is (12 + 28) / 2 = 20, e3. Every other move clears it, because the right to capture en passant lasts one move only.
  • Finally the side to move flips. Note that make_move never checks anything: it trusts that the move came from the generator. Checking is the next step's job.

7Legal or not?

Goal: reject any move that leaves your own king attacked, with no special code for pins.

Concept

A move is illegal if, afterwards, your king is attacked. Because copy-make has already built the child position, we can simply look: compute the opponent's attack map in the child, and check the king's square.

That one test handles everything that makes legality hard: pinned pieces, moving into check, failing to get out of check, and even the rare en-passant capture that opens a line along a rank. No pin detection is needed.

Castling adds one rule: the king may not start on, cross, or land on an attacked square. So for castling we test three squares instead of one. Those three are always consecutive, so they are 7 << min(from, to): e1-g1 tests squares 4, 5, 6, and e1-c1 tests 2, 3, 4.

You might wonder whether the castling test is right, since it looks at the child, where the king and rook have already moved. It is. If an attacker's ray reaches f1 after castling, it passes through the now-empty e1 or comes from elsewhere, and either way that same attacker already covered f1 or e1 before castling. The perft tests in Step 9 confirm it.

Code
Add to c/chess.hpart 7 of 18
/* After move m, is the mover's king safe? "child" is the position after
 * the move, so the mover is the side that is NOT to move in it. */
static inline int legal_after(const Position *child, Move m) {
    int mover = !child->side;
    int from = MOVE_FROM(m), to = MOVE_TO(m);
    U64 safe = child->bb[mover * 6 + KING];

    /* Castling: start, crossed and final squares must all be safe. */
    if (safe == BIT(to) && (to == from + 2 || to == from - 2))
        safe = (U64)7 << (from < to ? from : to);

    return (side_attacks(child, child->side) & safe) == 0;
}

Line by line

  • child is the position after the move, so the player who just moved is the one not to move: mover = !child->side.
  • safe starts as the mover's king. For a normal move, that is the only square that must not be attacked.
  • For castling (the king landed on to, two squares from from), three squares must be safe: where the king started (you cannot castle out of check), the square it crossed, and where it landed. (U64)7 << min(from, to) is three set bits starting at the lower square. For e1g1 that is squares 4, 5 and 6: e1, f1, g1. For e1c1 it is 2, 3 and 4: c1, d1, e1. (b1 must be empty but may be attacked; the generator checks it is empty.)
  • Finally, compute the attack map of the side now to move, the opponent, and check that none of those squares is in it.

8Generating moves, in a good order

Goal: list every move, with the moves most likely to be good coming first.

Concept

The search in Step 13 becomes dramatically faster when it tries good moves first. Instead of generating moves and then sorting them, we generate them in a good order from the start, in seven stages:

StageMovesWhy this order
0pawn pushes that promotealmost always strong
1 to 5captures of a queen, rook, bishop, knight, then pawn (including en passant)take the most valuable victim first
6everything else, including castling"quiet" moves

Inside each stage we visit our pieces from pawn up to king. So within "capture a queen", a pawn takes the queen before a queen does. Together that is a classic rule called most valuable victim, least valuable attacker. Promotions come out as queen, rook, bishop, then knight.

This exact order is part of the specification: the hardware must write exactly the same list, in exactly the same order. That makes the tests in Part 2 very strong, because one move out of place shows up immediately.

These are pseudo-legal moves: they obey how pieces move, but are not yet checked for king safety. The search checks each move only when it actually tries it (Step 7). At a node that cuts off after its first move, the other legality tests are never needed.

Code

First, one function that answers "where can this one piece go, in this stage?". Pawn pushes are special (they are not attacks), so they come first. Every other piece starts from its attack set: in the quiet stage keep the empty squares, in a capture stage keep only the squares holding that stage's victim.

Add to c/chess.hpart 8 of 18
/* Generation stages, in the order the search will try them. */
enum { ST_PROMO, ST_CAP_Q, ST_CAP_R, ST_CAP_B, ST_CAP_N, ST_CAP_P, ST_QUIET };

/* Destinations of ONE piece (the single bit in from_bit) in one stage. */
static inline U64 stage_targets(const Position *p, int stage, int type, U64 from_bit) {
    int us = p->side;
    U64 occ = occupied(p);
    U64 att, victims;

    /* Pawn pushes: promotions in ST_PROMO, the rest in ST_QUIET. */
    if (stage == ST_PROMO || (stage == ST_QUIET && type == PAWN)) {
        int up = us == WHITE ? 8 : -8;
        U64 one, two;
        if (type != PAWN) return 0;
        one = shift(from_bit, up) & ~occ;
        if (stage == ST_PROMO) return one & (RANK_1 | RANK_8);
        two = shift(one, up) & ~occ & (us == WHITE ? RANK_4 : RANK_5);
        return (one & ~(RANK_1 | RANK_8)) | two;
    }

    switch (type) {
    case PAWN:   att = pawn_attacks(us, from_bit);                     break;
    case KNIGHT: att = knight_attacks(from_bit);                       break;
    case BISHOP: att = bishop_attacks(from_bit, occ);                  break;
    case ROOK:   att = rook_attacks(from_bit, occ);                    break;
    case QUEEN:  att = bishop_attacks(from_bit, occ)
                     | rook_attacks(from_bit, occ);                    break;
    default:     att = king_attacks(from_bit);                         break;
    }

    if (stage == ST_QUIET) {
        U64 t = att & ~occ;
        if (type == KING) {           /* castling: right + empty squares */
            if (us == WHITE) {
                if ((p->castle & WK) && !(occ & 0x60ULL)) t |= BIT(6);
                if ((p->castle & WQ) && !(occ & 0x0EULL)) t |= BIT(2);
            } else {
                if ((p->castle & BK) && !(occ & (0x60ULL << 56))) t |= BIT(62);
                if ((p->castle & BQ) && !(occ & (0x0EULL << 56))) t |= BIT(58);
            }
        }
        return t;
    }

    /* Capture stages ST_CAP_Q..ST_CAP_P pick the victim QUEEN..PAWN. */
    victims = p->bb[(!us) * 6 + QUEEN - (stage - ST_CAP_Q)];
    if (stage == ST_CAP_P && type == PAWN && p->ep != NO_EP)
        victims |= BIT(p->ep);
    return att & victims;
}

Line by line

  1. The function answers one question: "where can this one piece go, in this stage?" from_bit has exactly one bit set.
  2. Pawn pushes are handled first, because they are the only moves that are not attacks. one is the square ahead if it is empty. In the promotion stage, keep it only if it is on the last rank. In the quiet stage, keep it only if it is not on the last rank (that move was already made as a promotion), plus two: one more step, only from the starting rank, which is why it is masked with rank 4 (White) or 5 (Black).
  3. Any piece type other than a pawn has no moves in the promotion stage, hence return 0.
  4. For everything else, att is the set of squares the piece attacks, from Steps 3 and 4. A queen is a bishop plus a rook.
  5. Quiet stage: attacked squares that are empty. The king adds castling: the right must still exist and the squares between king and rook must be empty (0x60 is f1 and g1; 0x0E is b1, c1 and d1).
  6. Capture stages: QUEEN - (stage - ST_CAP_Q) picks the victim type: the queen stage takes queens, the next rooks, and so on down to pawns. The answer is attacks that land on a victim. In the pawn stage, a pawn may also "capture" the en-passant square, which is empty.

The castling check here only looks at the right and the empty squares between king and rook. Whether those squares are attacked is legal_after's job.

Then the generator itself. It is four nested loops, and in Part 2 each loop becomes one register in the hardware:

Expected output
for each stage                         -> register "stage"
  for each piece type                  -> register "ptype"
    for each piece of that type        -> register "pieces"  (lowest bit first)
      for each destination             -> register "targets" (lowest bit first)
        write the move
Add to c/chess.hpart 9 of 18
/* Write pseudo-legal moves to list; return how many. The order is fixed:
 * promotions, captures (best victim, then cheapest attacker), quiet moves.
 * captures_only stops before the quiet stage (used by quiescence). */
static inline int generate_moves(const Position *p, Move *list, int captures_only) {
    const U64 *mine = p->bb + p->side * 6;
    int last_stage = captures_only ? ST_CAP_P : ST_QUIET;
    int n = 0, stage, type;

    for (stage = ST_PROMO; stage <= last_stage; stage++) {
        for (type = PAWN; type <= KING; type++) {
            U64 pieces = mine[type];
            while (pieces) {
                int from = lsb(pieces);
                U64 targets = stage_targets(p, stage, type, BIT(from));
                pieces &= pieces - 1;               /* next piece next time */
                while (targets) {
                    int to = lsb(targets);
                    targets &= targets - 1;
                    if (type == PAWN && (BIT(to) & (RANK_1 | RANK_8))) {
                        int promo;
                        for (promo = QUEEN; promo >= KNIGHT; promo--)
                            list[n++] = MAKE_MOVE(from, to, promo);
                    } else {
                        list[n++] = MAKE_MOVE(from, to, 0);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return n;
}

Line by line

  1. Three nested loops: stage, then piece type from pawn to king, then each piece of that type. That nesting is the move order: all queen captures by pawns, then by knights, ..., then all rook captures, and so on.
  2. lsb(pieces) takes the lowest piece; pieces &= pieces - 1 removes it (Step 2's trick). The same two lines walk through targets.
  3. A pawn reaching rank 1 or 8 produces four moves, queen first, because the queen is almost always the best choice and should be searched first.
  4. captures_only stops after the last capture stage. Quiescence uses it: it only looks at captures.
  5. The moves are pseudo-legal: they may leave the king in check. Checking is done later, one move at a time, by legal_after. Most of the time the search cuts off before it reaches the illegal ones, so that work is never done.

9Proving the rules with perft

Goal: prove that steps 1 to 8 are exactly right before writing any search.

Concept

Perft counts every legal sequence of moves to a fixed depth. From the start position there are 20 legal first moves, 400 two-move sequences, 8,902 three-move sequences, and so on. These counts have been published for many test positions, so they are a perfect check: perft has no evaluation and no pruning, so a wrong count can only mean a rules bug.

Expected output
perft(position, 0) = 1
perft(position, d) = sum over each legal move of perft(child, d - 1)
Code

Perft is the simplest recursive function in the engine, and it shows the shape every search will have: generate, copy, make, test legality, recurse.

Add to c/chess.hpart 10 of 18
/* Count every legal move sequence of exactly "depth" moves. */
static inline uint64_t perft(const Position *p, int depth) {
    Move list[MAX_MOVES];
    uint64_t leaves = 0;
    int n, i;
    if (depth == 0) return 1;
    n = generate_moves(p, list, 0);
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        Position child = *p;                  /* copy ...  */
        make_move(&child, list[i]);           /* ... make  */
        if (legal_after(&child, list[i]))
            leaves += perft(&child, depth - 1);
    }
    return leaves;
}

Line by line

  1. At depth 0 the current position is one leaf: return 1.
  2. Otherwise generate every pseudo-legal move. For each one, copy the position, make the move on the copy, and keep it only if the mover's king is safe.
  3. Add up the leaves under every legal move. The recursion goes as deep as depth; each level has its own list and child on the C stack.
  4. Copy-make means there is no "unmake": the parent position *p is never changed, so nothing can be restored wrongly. A position is only 100 bytes, so copying it is cheap.

To test real positions we need to read FEN, the standard one-line text format for a chess position. A FEN has four fields we care about: the pieces rank by rank from rank 8 (digits mean empty squares), the side to move, castling rights, and the en-passant square:

Expected output
rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1
\_____________ pieces ____________________/ |  |    |
                                  side to move  |    en passant
                                         castling
Add to c/chess.hpart 11 of 18
/* Read a FEN string such as
 * "rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1".
 * Returns 1 on success, 0 if the text is not a usable position. */
static inline int from_fen(const char *fen, Position *p) {
    static const char symbols[] = "PNBRQKpnbrqk";
    const char *s = fen;
    int file = 0, rank = 7;

    memset(p, 0, sizeof *p);
    p->ep = NO_EP;

    /* 1. Pieces, from a8 to h1. */
    for (; *s && *s != ' '; s++) {
        const char *hit = strchr(symbols, *s);
        if (*s == '/') {
            file = 0;
            rank--;
        } else if (*s >= '1' && *s <= '8') {
            file += *s - '0';
        } else if (hit) {
            if (file > 7 || rank < 0) return 0;
            p->bb[hit - symbols] |= BIT(rank * 8 + file);
            file++;
        } else {
            return 0;
        }
    }

    /* 2. Side to move. */
    while (*s == ' ') s++;
    if (*s != 'w' && *s != 'b') return 0;
    p->side = *s == 'w' ? WHITE : BLACK;
    s++;

Line by line: the board field

  1. memset clears all twelve boards, the side, the rights; then ep is set to NO_EP, because 0 would mean "a1".
  2. A FEN board lists rank 8 first, from the a-file to the h-file, so we start at rank = 7, file = 0.
  3. / moves down one rank and back to the a-file. A digit skips that many empty squares.
  4. A letter is looked up in "PNBRQKpnbrqk". Its position in that string is exactly its board index: P is 0 (white pawns), k is 11 (black king). strchr returns a pointer into the string, and hit - symbols turns it into that index. The square number is rank * 8 + file, as in Step 1.
  5. Any other character, or a piece beyond the board edge, means the text is broken: return 0.

The remaining fields are short. Each one is separated by spaces, so each part starts by skipping them.

Add to c/chess.hpart 12 of 18
    /* 3. Castling rights. */
    while (*s == ' ') s++;
    for (; *s && *s != ' '; s++) {
        if (*s == 'K') p->castle |= WK;
        if (*s == 'Q') p->castle |= WQ;
        if (*s == 'k') p->castle |= BK;
        if (*s == 'q') p->castle |= BQ;
    }
    /* A right only counts if the king and rook are really at home. */
    if (!(p->bb[KING] & BIT(4)))      p->castle &= ~(WK | WQ);
    if (!(p->bb[6 + KING] & BIT(60))) p->castle &= ~(BK | BQ);
    if (!(p->bb[ROOK] & BIT(7)))      p->castle &= ~WK;
    if (!(p->bb[ROOK] & BIT(0)))      p->castle &= ~WQ;
    if (!(p->bb[6 + ROOK] & BIT(63))) p->castle &= ~BK;
    if (!(p->bb[6 + ROOK] & BIT(56))) p->castle &= ~BQ;

    /* 4. En-passant square, such as "e3", or "-". */
    while (*s == ' ') s++;
    if (*s == '\0') return 0;
    if (*s != '-') {
        if (s[0] < 'a' || s[0] > 'h' || s[1] < '1' || s[1] > '8') return 0;
        p->ep = (s[1] - '1') * 8 + (s[0] - 'a');
    }

    /* 5. Exactly one king each, and the side that just moved is not in check. */
    if (count_bits(p->bb[KING]) != 1 || count_bits(p->bb[6 + KING]) != 1) return 0;
    return (side_attacks(p, p->side) & p->bb[(!p->side) * 6 + KING]) == 0;
}

Line by line: the other fields

  1. Castling: each letter sets one right. - sets none. Then the six checks throw away any right whose king or rook is not on its starting square: a hand-written FEN can claim rights the board cannot have, and the move generator trusts the rights.
  2. En passant: - or a square name such as e3. (s[1] - '1') * 8 + (s[0] - 'a') converts it to 20.
  3. The half-move and full-move counters at the end are not needed by the engine, so they are not read.
  4. Sanity: exactly one king each (count_bits), and the side that just moved must not be in check. That second test catches positions where the wrong side is "to move".

from_fen also rejects impossible positions: a missing king, or a position where the side that just moved is still in check. Then one small helper turns a move word into text such as e2e4:

Add to c/chess.hpart 13 of 18
/* Write a move as text: "e2e4", "a7a8q", or "none" for move 0. */
static inline void move_to_text(Move m, char text[6]) {
    if (m == 0) {
        strcpy(text, "none");
        return;
    }
    text[0] = (char)('a' + (MOVE_FROM(m) & 7));
    text[1] = (char)('1' + (MOVE_FROM(m) >> 3));
    text[2] = (char)('a' + (MOVE_TO(m) & 7));
    text[3] = (char)('1' + (MOVE_TO(m) >> 3));
    text[4] = MOVE_PROMO(m) ? " nbrq"[MOVE_PROMO(m)] : '\0';
    text[5] = '\0';
}

Now the test program. It holds six well-known positions with their published counts, from the Chess Programming Wiki. Each one stresses different rules:

PositionWhat it stresses
startnormal play
kiwipetecastling, pins, en passant, tactics
pos3en passant that exposes the king along a rank
pos4promotions, castling after captures
pos5promotion with check, castling rights
pos6a busy, normal middlegame
Create c/main.cpart 1 of 2
/* main.c - command-line tool for the golden engine.
 *   engine test                      check 30 published perft counts
 *   engine perft  "<fen>" <depth>    count moves, split by first move
 *   engine search "<fen>" <depth>    search depth 1, 2, ... depth      */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include "chess.h"

#define START_FEN "rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1"

typedef struct {
    const char *name;
    const char *fen;
    uint64_t expected[5];          /* perft counts for depth 1 to 5 */
} PerftCase;

static const PerftCase PERFT_CASES[] = {
    {"start", START_FEN,
        {20, 400, 8902, 197281, 4865609}},
    {"kiwipete", "r3k2r/p1ppqpb1/bn2pnp1/3PN3/1p2P3/2N2Q1p/PPPBBPPP/R3K2R w KQkq - 0 1",
        {48, 2039, 97862, 4085603, 193690690}},
    {"pos3", "8/2p5/3p4/KP5r/1R3p1k/8/4P1P1/8 w - - 0 1",
        {14, 191, 2812, 43238, 674624}},
    {"pos4", "r3k2r/Pppp1ppp/1b3nbN/nP6/BBP1P3/q4N2/Pp1P2PP/R2Q1RK1 w kq - 0 1",
        {6, 264, 9467, 422333, 15833292}},
    {"pos5", "rnbq1k1r/pp1Pbppp/2p5/8/2B5/8/PPP1NnPP/RNBQK2R w KQ - 1 8",
        {44, 1486, 62379, 2103487, 89941194}},
    {"pos6", "r4rk1/1pp1qppp/p1np1n2/2b1p1B1/2B1P1b1/P1NP1N2/1PP1QPPP/R4RK1 w - - 0 10",
        {46, 2079, 89890, 3894594, 164075551}},
};

static int run_tests(void) {
    int failures = 0, c, d;
    for (c = 0; c < 6; c++) {
        Position p;
        from_fen(PERFT_CASES[c].fen, &p);
        for (d = 1; d <= 5; d++) {
            uint64_t got = perft(&p, d);
            int ok = got == PERFT_CASES[c].expected[d - 1];
            printf("%-9s depth %d  %11llu  %s\n", PERFT_CASES[c].name, d,
                   (unsigned long long)got, ok ? "ok" : "FAIL");
            if (!ok) failures++;
        }
    }
    if (failures) printf("FAILED: %d mismatches\n", failures);
    else          printf("ALL PERFT TESTS PASSED\n");
    return failures != 0;
}

Line by line

  1. Each PerftCase is a name, a FEN, and the published correct counts for depths 1 to 5. These numbers come from the Chess Programming Wiki's perft results and have been confirmed by many independent engines.
  2. run_tests loads each position, runs perft at depths 1 to 5, and prints one line per depth with ok or FAIL.
  3. It returns non-zero if anything failed, so a script or a build tool can stop on a broken engine.

And main, which also gives us a "divide" command for debugging and, later, a search command:

Add to c/main.cpart 2 of 2
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    Position p;
    int depth;
    clock_t start = clock();

    if (argc < 2 || strcmp(argv[1], "test") == 0) return run_tests();
    if (argc < 4) {
        printf("usage: engine test | perft \"<fen>\" <depth> | search \"<fen>\" <depth>\n");
        return 1;
    }
    if (!from_fen(argv[2], &p)) {
        printf("invalid FEN\n");
        return 1;
    }
    depth = atoi(argv[3]);

    if (strcmp(argv[1], "perft") == 0) {
        /* "Divide": the count under each first move, then the total. */
        Move list[MAX_MOVES];
        uint64_t total = 0;
        int n = generate_moves(&p, list, 0), i;
        for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            Position child = p;
            char text[6];
            make_move(&child, list[i]);
            if (!legal_after(&child, list[i])) continue;
            uint64_t count = perft(&child, depth - 1);
            move_to_text(list[i], text);
            printf("%-6s %llu\n", text, (unsigned long long)count);
            total += count;
        }
        printf("total  %llu\n", (unsigned long long)total);
    } else if (strcmp(argv[1], "search") == 0) {
        int d;
        for (d = 1; d <= depth; d++) {
            SearchResult r = search(&p, d, 0);
            char text[6];
            move_to_text(r.best, text);
            printf("depth %2d  best %-6s score %6d  nodes %llu\n",
                   d, text, r.score, (unsigned long long)r.nodes);
        }
    }
    printf("time %.3f s\n", (double)(clock() - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);
    return 0;
}

10Evaluating a position

Goal: turn any position into one number: how good it is for the side to move.

Concept

When the search stops looking ahead, it needs a guess at who is better. Scores are in centipawns: a pawn is worth 100. We use the well-known Simplified Evaluation Function by Tomasz Michniewski, which has two parts:

  • Material: pawn 100, knight 320, bishop 330, rook 500, queen 900.
  • Piece-square tables: a bonus or penalty for every piece on every square. Knights like the center, pawns like to advance, the king likes to hide in a corner.

The king gets two tables. While any queen is on the board, it should stay sheltered. Once both queens are gone the danger drops, and it should walk to the center to help in the endgame. That is a single, simple rule, and in hardware it is one wire.

The tables are written like a printed board, rank 8 on the first row. A white piece on square sq reads entry sq ^ 56. XOR with 56 flips the rank (e2 is square 12, and 12 ^ 56 = 52, which is the row for rank 2). A black piece reads entry sq directly, which mirrors the board, so both sides see the table from their own end.

Two more details. Tempo: the side to move gets 10 extra, for having the move. Sign: the final score is from the point of view of the side to move: positive is good for whoever is about to move. The next steps explain why that makes the search simpler.

This evaluator is weak by modern standards: it knows nothing about mobility, pawn structure or king safety. It is chosen because it suits hardware perfectly. Each square's contribution depends only on what stands on that square, so all 64 can be computed at the same moment, then added up with a tree of adders.

Code

First the numbers. PIECE_VALUE is the material value of each type in centipawns. PST holds seven 64-entry tables: one per piece type, plus a second king table for the endgame. They are written as you would see the board from White's side, rank 8 on the first line.

Add to c/chess.hpart 14 of 18

 * A white piece on square sq uses PST[type][sq ^ 56]; a black one uses
 * PST[type][sq], which mirrors the table for Black. */

#define TEMPO 10          /* small bonus for having the move */

Then the function that adds them up:

Add to c/chess.hpart 15 of 18
/* Score in centipawns (pawn = 100) from the side to move's point of view. */
static inline int evaluate(const Position *p) {
    int endgame = (p->bb[QUEEN] | p->bb[6 + QUEEN]) == 0;
    int white_minus_black = 0, pc;

    for (pc = 0; pc < 12; pc++) {
        int type  = pc % 6;
        int table = (type == KING && endgame) ? 6 : type;
        U64 b = p->bb[pc];
        while (b) {
            int sq = lsb(b);
            b &= b - 1;
            if (pc < 6) white_minus_black += PIECE_VALUE[type] + PST[table][sq ^ 56];
            else        white_minus_black -= PIECE_VALUE[type] + PST[table][sq];
        }
    }
    white_minus_black += p->side == WHITE ? TEMPO : -TEMPO;
    return p->side == WHITE ? white_minus_black : -white_minus_black;
}

Line by line

  1. Endgame? Here simply "no queens on the board". It only changes which king table is used: in the middlegame the king should hide, in the endgame it should come to the centre.
  2. The loop visits every piece on the board. For each one, it adds its material value and its square bonus to a running "White minus Black" total.
  3. sq ^ 56 for White. The tables are printed rank 8 first, so entry 0 is the top-left corner, a8, and entries 56 to 63 are the bottom row, rank 1. A white piece on a1 (square 0) must read the bottom row, so its index is flipped: 0 ^ 56 = 56. XOR with 56 flips the rank and keeps the file. A black piece uses sq as it is: Black's back rank, squares 56 to 63, also lands on the bottom row. So both sides read "their own home row" from the same table, which mirrors it for free.
  4. The side to move gets a small bonus, TEMPO, for having the move.
  5. The last line turns "White minus Black" into "me minus you": negamax always wants the score from the side to move's point of view.

11The game tree, and minimax

Goal: understand how looking ahead turns many guesses into one good decision.

Concept

Picture every possible future as a tree. The current position is the root. Each legal move is a branch to a child position, each reply branches again, and so on. One move by one side is called a ply, so "depth 3" means three plies: my move, your reply, my move.

We can't search to the end of the game, so we stop at a fixed depth and evaluate the leaves. Then the scores flow back up the tree, under one assumption: both players always choose the move that is best for them.

  • At White's turns (MAX nodes), White picks the child with the highest score.
  • At Black's turns (MIN nodes), Black picks the child with the lowest score, since scores here are from White's side.

This is minimax. Step through it on a small tree: three moves at the root, two replies to each, two moves after that, then twelve leaves.

Look at what minimax finds. B, the first root move, contains a leaf worth 20, but White never gets it: Black would steer the game elsewhere. Minimax doesn't trust hope. It plays the line where the opponent defends as well as possible.

The cost is the problem. With about 35 legal moves in a typical position, depth 6 has 356, almost 1.8 billion, leaves. Steps 13 and 14 are about not visiting most of them.

A worked example, by hand

Take the smallest interesting tree: White has two moves, A and B, and Black has two replies to each. The leaves are scored from White's side.

Expected output
            root (White, MAX)
           /                 \
      A (Black, MIN)     B (Black, MIN)
       /      \           /      \
     +30     -10        +5      +8
  1. At A, Black chooses between +30 and −10. Black wants the lowest score, so A is worth −10. The +30 is a line White would love, but Black will never play into it.
  2. At B, Black chooses between +5 and +8, so B is worth +5.
  3. At the root, White chooses between A (−10) and B (+5), so the root is worth +5, and the move to play is B.

Notice that White picks B even though the best single leaf, +30, is under A. That is the "assume the opponent defends perfectly" rule at work.

How fast the tree grows

Real chess trees grow by a factor of about 35 per ply. The right-hand column is the exact number of positions at each depth from the starting position (the perft counts you will check in Step 9):

Depth35depthReal positions from the start
13520
21,225400

61,838,265,625119,060,324

The opening has fewer moves than a typical middlegame, so the real numbers are smaller, but the growth is the same story: every extra ply multiplies the work by twenty to forty.

12Negamax: one rule instead of two

Goal: write minimax as a single function with no "if White ... else Black".

Concept

Chess is zero-sum: what is good for me is exactly that bad for you. If a position is worth +3 to Black, it is worth −3 to White. So if every score is given from the point of view of the side to move (which is how evaluate already works), the MIN rule disappears:

score(position) = maximum over moves of −score(child)

The minus sign switches perspective at every level. The child's score is from the opponent's side, so negating it gives my side. Every node becomes a MAX node. Switch the figure to the negamax view: the tree is the same, only the signs at the MIN levels change, and the root's answer is identical.

The worked example again, in negamax

Same tree as in Step 11. Now every leaf is scored from the side to move at that leaf. After A or B and a black reply it is White's move again, so the leaves keep their values: +30, −10, +5, +8.

  1. At A it is Black's move. Black takes the maximum of the negated children: max(−30, +10) = +10. From Black's side, A is worth +10.
  2. At B: max(−5, −8) = −5.
  3. At the root it is White's move: max(−(+10), −(−5)) = max(−10, +5) = +5, move B.

Same answer, +5 and move B, but there was only one rule, "take the maximum of the negated children", at every node. That is what lets the C, and later the hardware state machine, use one piece of code for both colours.

In code, negamax is about ten lines. This is the core of the engine, before any speed-ups:

C
int negamax(const Position *p, int depth) {
    if (depth == 0) return evaluate(p);       /* a leaf                      */
    int best = -INF;
    for each legal move m {
        Position child = *p;  make_move(&child, m);
        int score = -negamax(&child, depth - 1);  /* the child's view, negated */
        if (score > best) best = score;
    }
    return best;
}

13Alpha-beta: skipping what can't matter

Goal: get exactly the minimax answer while visiting far fewer leaves.

Concept

Imagine you are choosing between three restaurants, and a friend picks your dish at each one, always the worst on the menu. You check restaurant B fully: its worst dish is fine, call it 12. At restaurant C, the first dish you look at is terrible, 8. Do you need to read the rest of C's menu? No. Your friend can already give you an 8 there, which is worse than the 12 you are sure of at B. C is ruled out, whatever else is on its menu.

That is the whole idea of alpha-beta pruning. While searching, carry two numbers down the tree:

  • α (alpha): the score MAX is already sure of, from moves searched earlier. MAX will never accept less.
  • β (beta): the score MIN is already sure of. MIN will never allow more.

Only scores strictly between α and β can change any decision higher in the tree. As soon as a node proves its score is outside that window, the rest of its moves cannot matter, and we stop searching it. That is a cutoff.

Step through it. Watch the window [α, β] above each node, and the three cutoffs: two where MIN refuses to enter (at F and J), and one where MAX refuses (at C).

Three things to take away from the figure:

  1. The answer is exactly the minimax answer. Pruning never changes the root's value or the move it picks, only how much work it takes.
  2. A cutoff happens when α ≥ β. At that point this node's score is already too good (or too bad) for the player above to allow.
  3. Order matters enormously. With the best move first, the very first child sets a tight window, and later siblings are cut off almost immediately.

Alpha-beta in negamax form

Our code uses negamax, so how does the window work there? When we go down one level, the opponent's view of the same window is negated and swapped:

Expected output
my window            [ alpha,  beta ]
child's window       [ -beta, -alpha ]

Why? If I already have α, my opponent knows I will refuse any line worth less than α to me, which is more than −α to them. So −α becomes their upper bound, their β. And the rule "stop when α ≥ β" is the same at every node, because every node is a MAX node. That gives the loop body you will see in Step 16:

C
score = -negamax(&child, depth - 1, -beta, -alpha, ply + 1);
if (score > best)  best = score;
if (score > alpha) alpha = score;
if (alpha >= beta) break;            /* cutoff: the rest cannot matter */

The cutoff on the worked example

Go back to the tree from Step 11 and search B first this time (B, then A):

  1. The root starts with the window [−∞, +∞]. It searches B fully: B is worth +5 to White, as before. The root's α becomes +5: White is now sure of at least +5.
  2. The root moves on to A, passing the window down negated and swapped: [−β, −α] = [−∞, −5]. In words, Black at A is told: "White already has +5 elsewhere, so anything worse than −5 for you is irrelevant".
  3. A's first reply leads to the leaf +30, which is −30 from Black's side. A's α becomes −30. Not yet ≥ −5, so carry on.
  4. A's second reply leads to −10, which is +10 from Black's side. A's α becomes +10. Now α (+10) ≥ β (−5): cutoff. A stops. (Here it was the last move anyway; with more replies, every remaining one would be skipped.)
  5. A returns +10, the root sees −10, which does not beat +5, so the answer is still +5 and move B.

Now imagine A had thirty replies and the strong one came first. Black's first reply would already reach α ≥ β, and the other twenty-nine would never be searched. That is where the savings come from, and why the order of moves matters so much.

14Why move order matters so much

Goal: see why Step 8 generates captures first.

Concept

On the small tree the savings looked modest. On real trees they are enormous, but only if good moves come first. With perfect ordering, alpha-beta needs about bd/2 leaves instead of bd: the square root. In the same time, it searches roughly twice as deep.

The numbers behind "square root"

Knuth and Moore proved in 1975 that with perfect ordering, alpha-beta visits b⌈d/2⌉ + b⌊d/2⌋ − 1 leaves. For 35 moves and depth 6 that is 42,875 + 42,875 − 1 = 85,749 leaves, against 1.8 billion for plain minimax: twenty thousand times fewer. With the worst ordering, alpha-beta cuts nothing and visits all 1.8 billion.

No engine knows the best move in advance; that is what it is searching for. But cheap rules get close:

  • Captures first, biggest victim first (MVV-LVA, Step 8). Winning material is often best, and even when it is not, a capture quickly raises α.
  • Promotions before everything. A new queen is worth 800 centipawns.
  • Killer moves (Part 5). A quiet move that caused a cutoff in a sibling position probably refutes this one too.

Real numbers from this engine, at depth 6 from the start position: the version you are building visits 1,519,394 nodes. In Part 5 we add one ordering idea, the killer move, and the same search visits 159,788 nodes, nine and a half times fewer, with exactly the same result. That is why the generator works so hard to put captures of valuable pieces first.

15The horizon, and quiescence

Goal: stop the engine from being fooled at the edge of its search.

Concept

A fixed depth creates a blind spot. Suppose the search stops right after my queen takes a pawn. The evaluator counts material and sees me a pawn up. It cannot see that the pawn was defended and my queen is lost on the very next move. Beyond the depth limit, the engine is blind. This is called the horizon effect.

The cure is quiescence search: when the normal depth runs out, don't evaluate straight away. Keep searching, but only captures and promotions, until the position is quiet. Two rules make it work:

  1. Stand pat. The side to move doesn't have to capture. So evaluate first: that score is a floor. If it is already at least β, stop at once. Otherwise raise α to it and try the captures.
  2. Not in check. In check, you can't "stand pat", because you must answer the check. So in check, search every legal reply. If there are none, it is checkmate.

Quiescence ends naturally: captures remove pieces, so capture sequences are short. And since moves come out "most valuable victim first", the strongest captures are tried first and cutoffs come quickly.

The trap from the figure, step by step

White's queen on h2 can take the pawn on e5, but the pawn on d6 defends it.

  1. Without quiescence, at depth 1: White plays Qxe5 and the search stops. evaluate counts material: White has won a pawn, so the score goes up by about 100 centipawns, and Qxe5 looks like the best move.
  2. With quiescence: after Qxe5 the depth is 0, but instead of evaluating at once the engine calls quiesce. It is Black's move. Stand pat first: the evaluation as it stands, with White a pawn richer, is Black's floor.
  3. Then Black tries the captures. dxe5 takes the queen. Now it is White's move, again in quiescence. White's stand-pat score has dropped by about 900 (the queen), and White has no capture back, so that is the value of the line.
  4. For Black, dxe5 is far better than standing pat, so Black takes the queen. Passed back up, Qxe5 is now worth about 800 centipawns less to White than not capturing at all (a queen lost, a pawn won). The engine plays something else.

One extra ply of captures-only search turned a blunder into a refused move, at a tiny cost: a capture sequence rarely runs more than a few moves deep.

16The search, in code

Goal: put negamax, alpha-beta, quiescence, and mate scores together in one function.

Concept

Two details remain.

Mate and stalemate. If a node has no legal move at all, it is checkmate if the side to move is in check, and stalemate (a draw, score 0) if not. Checkmate at ply p scores −MATE + p. A quicker mate is worth slightly more, so the engine plays the fastest win and the slowest defence.

A depth limit for the stack. The hardware stack holds 32 plies. Quiescence can, in theory, go very deep, so at ply 31 we stop and return the evaluation. The C does the same, so both always visit exactly the same nodes.

Every variable in negamax that must survive the recursive call (alpha, beta, best, the loop index, any_legal, check) becomes a field in the hardware's stack frame in Part 2. Keep an eye on them.

Code

The result type, plus counters that live outside the recursion. The node limit lets the CPU stop a search that is taking too long; the hardware has the same feature.

Add to c/chess.hpart 16 of 18
#define INF  32000        /* bigger than any real score     */
#define MATE 30000        /* score for giving checkmate     */

typedef struct {
    Move     best;        /* 0 means no legal move (mate or stalemate) */
    int      score;
    uint64_t nodes;
    int      aborted;     /* 1 if the node limit stopped the search    */
} SearchResult;

/* The search keeps its bookkeeping here, outside the recursion. */
static SearchResult search_result;
static uint64_t     search_node_limit;     /* 0 = no limit */

Line by line

  1. INF is larger than any score the evaluation can produce, so -INF is a safe "worse than anything" starting value. MATE is below INF and above any material score.
  2. SearchResult is everything the caller gets back. best is the move at the root; 0 means there is no legal move.
  3. The two static variables are shared by every level of the recursion: the node counter and the limit. Keeping them outside negamax keeps its argument list short; the hardware keeps them in single registers for the same reason.

And the heart of the engine. Read it top to bottom alongside Steps 12 to 15. Every line has a reason you've already seen.

Add to c/chess.hpart 17 of 18
/* Fail-soft negamax alpha-beta with quiescence. rtl/search_core.sv
 * performs exactly this recursion, one state per clock. */
static inline int negamax(const Position *p, int depth, int alpha, int beta, int ply) {
    Move list[MAX_MOVES];
    int check, quiesce, stand_pat, best, n, i, any_legal = 0;

    search_result.nodes++;
    if (search_node_limit && search_result.nodes >= search_node_limit) {
        search_result.aborted = 1;
        return 0;
    }

    check = in_check(p);
    if (ply == MAX_PLY - 1) return evaluate(p);     /* the stack is full */

    quiesce   = depth == 0;
    stand_pat = quiesce && !check;
    best = -INF;
    if (stand_pat) {                 /* may refuse every capture */
        best = evaluate(p);
        if (best >= beta) return best;
        if (best > alpha) alpha = best;
    }

    n = generate_moves(p, list, stand_pat);
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        Position child = *p;
        int score;
        make_move(&child, list[i]);
        if (!legal_after(&child, list[i])) continue;
        any_legal = 1;

        score = -negamax(&child, quiesce ? 0 : depth - 1, -beta, -alpha, ply + 1);
        if (search_result.aborted) return 0;

        if (score > best) {
            best = score;
            if (ply == 0) search_result.best = list[i];
        }
        if (score > alpha) alpha = score;
        if (alpha >= beta) break;     /* cutoff: the rest cannot matter */
    }

    if (!any_legal && !stand_pat)     /* no legal move at all */
        return check ? -MATE + ply : 0;
    return best;
}

Line by line

  1. Count the node, check the limit. If the limit is reached, set aborted and return 0. Every caller checks aborted right after its recursive call, so the whole search unwinds immediately and the half-finished answer is never used.
  2. In check? Computed once; it decides whether this node may stand pat and whether "no legal moves" means mate or stalemate.
  3. The deepest ply simply returns the evaluation: the hardware has 32 stack rows, so the C stops at the same depth.
  4. Quiescence (depth == 0): if not in check, the side to move may "stand pat", meaning decline every capture and accept the static evaluation. That value is a lower bound on this node's score, so it may cause an immediate cutoff, or raise alpha.
  5. Generate all moves, or captures only when standing pat. In check, all moves are generated even at depth 0, because every escape must be considered.
  6. The loop: copy, make, skip illegal moves. any_legal records that at least one move was legal.
  7. The recursive call searches the child with the window negated and swapped: (-beta, -alpha). The minus sign in front turns the child's score, which is from the opponent's point of view, into ours. In quiescence the depth stays at 0.
  8. Update: a new best (remembering the move at the root), a raised alpha, and the cutoff: once alpha >= beta, the opponent already has a better option elsewhere and will never allow this position, so the remaining moves cannot matter.
  9. No legal move at a node that was not standing pat: checkmate if in check (-MATE + ply: losing later is less bad), otherwise stalemate, a draw.

Two details worth noticing. The score is "fail-soft": a node can return a value outside its window, not just α or β, which gives slightly better information to the level above. And the root's best move is recorded whenever a root move beats best.

Finally, the entry point, and the end of chess.h:

Add to c/chess.hpart 18 of 18
static inline SearchResult search(const Position *root, int depth, uint64_t node_limit) {
    memset(&search_result, 0, sizeof search_result);
    search_node_limit = node_limit;
    search_result.score = negamax(root, depth, -INF, INF, 0);
    return search_result;
}

#endif
