tb_search577 searches and perfts, 2.4 million nodes0 errors, 49.9 clocks per node
tb_axi40 searches, plus abort0 errors

Clocks per node depends on the position: 33 to 36 for depth 5 and 6 from the start, about 50 across the tactical test set. At 50 MHz that is 1 to 1.5 million nodes per second, from a few percent of the chip, against about 12,000 for the JavaScript in this page.

Part 2 checklist
  • All five testbenches print PASS under xsim.
  • You can explain why child can feed the attack test in S_ENTER.
  • You can point to where each negamax variable lives in the frame.
Part 3

On the PYNQ-Z2

From source files to a move on real silicon. Do the steps in order. Vivado's menus move a little between releases, so if a label differs, look for the closest match. This part could not be run while writing the guide, so each step says exactly what to expect: if something differs, trust what Vivado tells you, and check the troubleshooting tables at the end.

33Install the board files

Vivado needs the PYNQ-Z2 board files to know the board's DDR memory settings and how the Zynq processor is wired.

  1. Check whether they are already installed. Start Vivado, click Create Project, and press Next until the Default Part page. Open the Boards tab and search for pynq. If pynq-z2 appears, cancel and go to Step 34.
  2. Download the board files from TUL's PYNQ-Z2 page.
  3. Extract them to a folder without spaces, such as C:\Xilinx\boards\pynq-z2\A.0. It should contain a board.xml file.
  4. Tell Vivado where they are. Create or edit %APPDATA%\Xilinx\Vivado\init.tcl and add this line, using forward slashes even on Windows (the method described by element14):
    Tcl console
    set_param board.repoPaths [list "C:/Xilinx/boards/pynq-z2/A.0"]
  5. Restart Vivado and repeat check 1. You should now see pynq-z2.

34Create the Vivado project

  1. Start Vivado. Click Create Project, then Next.
  2. Project name: chess_pynq. Location: C:/chess/vivado. Keep Create project subdirectory ticked. Next.
  3. Project type: RTL Project, and tick Do not specify sources at this time. Next.
  4. Default Part: open the Boards tab, select pynq-z2, then Next and Finish.
  5. In the Flow Navigator on the left, under PROJECT MANAGER, click Add Sources. Choose Add or create design sources, Next.
  6. Click Add Files, go to C:\chess\rtl, select all seven files, and click OK.
  7. Untick Copy sources into project, so your edits in C:\chess\rtl are the ones that get built. Finish.
  8. In the Sources window, under Design Sources, you should see chess_axi_top with chess_axi, search_core and the rest beneath it.

Don't add the testbenches: you have already run them from the command line. If Vivado reports that chess_pkg is not declared, open the Compile Order tab in the Sources window and make sure chess_pkg.sv is first, with file type SystemVerilog.

35Draw the block design

The block design connects your core to the Zynq's processor system:

  1. In the Flow Navigator, under IP INTEGRATOR, click Create Block Design. Name it system, OK.
  2. Click + (Add IP) in the empty diagram, search for zynq, and double-click ZYNQ7 Processing System.
  3. Click Run Block Automation in the green banner. Leave Apply Board Preset ticked, and click OK. The DDR and FIXED_IO ports appear. This configures the board's DDR memory; without it, bare-metal programs won't run.
  4. Double-click the Zynq block:
    1. Open Clock Configuration, expand PL Fabric Clocks, tick FCLK_CLK0, and set Requested Frequency to 50.
    2. Open PS-PL Configuration, then AXI Non Secure Enablement, then GP Master AXI Interface, and make sure M AXI GP0 interface is ticked.
    3. Click OK.
  5. Right-click an empty part of the diagram and choose Add Module. Select chess_axi_top and click OK. A block named chess_axi_top_0 appears, with one s_axi bus port, aclk and aresetn.
  6. Click Run Connection Automation, tick All Automation, OK. Vivado adds an AXI Interconnect (or SmartConnect) and a Processor System Reset, and wires the clocks.
  7. Open the Address Editor tab. Find chess_axi_top_0: it should have a 4K range at an address such as 0x43C0_0000. Write this address down. Your software needs it.
  8. Press F6 (Validate Design). You want "Validation successful". Warnings about unused interrupts are fine; critical warnings are not.
  9. Save with Ctrl+S. In the Sources window, right-click system.bd, choose Create HDL Wrapper, then Let Vivado manage wrapper and auto-update, OK.
  10. system_wrapper should now be the top module, shown in bold. If not, right-click it and choose Set as Top.

What you just built, block by block

BlockIts job in the AXI path
ZYNQ7 Processing SystemThe Cortex-A9. Its M_AXI_GP0 port is an AXI master: every load or store the CPU makes to an address from 0x4000_0000 to 0x7FFF_FFFF leaves the processor through this port. FCLK_CLK0 is a clock it generates for the fabric.
AXI Interconnect / SmartConnectRoutes each transaction by address to the right slave, and converts the processor's full AXI3 protocol into the simpler AXI4-Lite your core speaks. With one slave it is almost a wire; with your GPU added (Step 42) it really routes.
Processor System ResetTakes the processor's reset and produces a clean, clock-synchronous peripheral_aresetn for the fabric. Your core's aresetn comes from here.
chess_axi_top_0Your core: an AXI4-Lite slave, answering at the address you assign it.

Check the AXI connection before going on

  1. Click the chess_axi_top_0 block. Its left side should show one bus port, s_axi, with a + next to it. Expand it: you should see the AWADDR, WDATA, BRESP, ARADDR and RDATA groups. That means Vivado inferred the AXI4-Lite interface from the port names. If instead you see 19 loose pins, the names don't match the convention: check chess_axi_top.v is the file you added.
  2. Hover over the aclk pin: the tooltip should list ASSOCIATED_BUSIF s_axi. If the clock and the bus were inferred separately, Validate (F6) warns that s_axi has no associated clock.
  3. Follow the wires: M_AXI_GP0 → interconnect S00_AXI; interconnect M00_AXI → chess_axi_top_0/s_axi; FCLK_CLK0 → M_AXI_GP0_ACLK, the interconnect clocks, and aclk; reset block peripheral_aresetn → aresetn.
  4. In the Address Editor, the row reads roughly: /chess_axi_top_0/s_axi, interface s_axi, base name reg0, Offset Address 0x43C0_0000, Range 4K. The core decodes 12 address bits, so 4K is exactly its size. If the row says "unassigned", right-click it and choose Assign.

If Validate complains

Message (roughly)Fix
"slave segment is not assigned into address space"Address Editor: right-click the row, Assign, then Validate again.
"interface s_axi has no associated clock" or a clock frequency mismatchMake sure aclk and the interconnect's M00_ACLK come from the same FCLK_CLK0. If the frequency differs, right-click the aclk pin, Properties, and check FREQ_HZ matches 50000000, or simply delete and redo Connection Automation.
"Module chess_axi_top not found" when adding the moduleThe rtl files must be in the project's design sources and chess_pkg.sv must be among them. Refresh the hierarchy (Sources window, right-click, Refresh Hierarchy).
Port width mismatch on awaddrNormal: the interconnect's 32-bit address is truncated to the core's 12 bits. Vivado does this for you; it is only an info message.

36Synthesize and read the reports

  1. Click Run Synthesis, then OK. It takes a few minutes.
  2. When it finishes, choose Open Synthesized Design.
  3. Open Reports, then Report Utilization, and click OK.

Compare with my estimate. These numbers came from Yosys, for the chess block alone; Vivado's will differ somewhat, and add the interconnect.

ResourceEstimateShare of the XC7Z020
LUTs11,42321%
Flip-flops4,2484%
RAMB36 block RAMs1611%
CARRY4141

Then check five things in the reports and the synthesis messages:

CheckGoodIf not
Block RAMabout 16 RAMB36 (or the same in RAMB18s)0 block RAM and thousands of extra flip-flops: the RAM was not inferred. Read the messages about mem in sdp_ram
Latchesnoneany "inferred latch" is a bug
Multi-driven netsnonea signal assigned in two places
LUT countthe same order as the estimateseveral times larger: the hierarchy view shows which block grew
Width warningsfew, and you can explain themlook hard at any on alpha, beta, score or ret

Warnings that s_axi_wstrb, s_axi_awprot and s_axi_arprot are unused are expected.

Reading the utilisation report

  • Slice LUTs is the main measure of logic. A 6-input LUT is a tiny lookup table that can compute any function of six inputs; the XC7Z020 has 53,200 of them. The chess core should use about a fifth, leaving plenty for your GPU.
  • Slice Registers are flip-flops: one per stored bit. The pos and child registers alone are over 1,500 of them.
  • Block RAM Tile counts 36 Kib RAMs. 16 is expected: 12 for the stack (because it is 851 bits wide) and 4 for the move lists.
  • Click Hierarchy in the report window to see the same numbers per module. Expect move_gen and search_core (with its attack tester) to be the two largest, and chess_axi to be small: it is mostly the 26 shadow registers.

37Implement, close timing, and write the bitstream

Run at 50 MHz first

  1. Click Run Implementation, then OK.
  2. When it's done, open Reports, then Timing, then Report Timing Summary.
  3. Read two numbers. WNS (worst negative slack) is the spare time on the slowest path; it must be zero or more. WHS (worst hold slack) must also be zero or more.

At 50 MHz each clock is 20 ns. My estimate puts the longest paths at about 12 logic levels; at very roughly 0.7 to 0.9 ns a level, 50 MHz should pass comfortably. That is an estimate, so read the real WNS.

Never ignore a negative WNS

A design that fails timing may seem to work, then return wrong moves at random. Fix it before you trust anything the board says.

How fast could it go?

Expected output
fastest period  ~ current period - WNS
fastest clock   ~ 1000 / fastest period    (MHz)

example: at 50 MHz, WNS = +8.2 ns  ->  20 - 8.2 = 11.8 ns  ->  about 85 MHz

To try a faster clock, double-click the Zynq block, open Clock Configuration, then PL Fabric Clocks, and set FCLK_CLK0 to the next target, say 75. Read the Actual Frequency column, since the processor can only make certain frequencies. Then run implementation again. The software reads the same clock counts at any speed: a faster clock just finishes sooner.

If timing fails

Don't hide it with false-path constraints. Find the real path: in Report Timing Summary, open Intra-Clock Paths, then the clock, then Setup, and double-click the worst path. Its Destination tells you where to look:

Destination containsPathFix
u_move_gen/targetssliding attacks for one piecesplit G_TARGETS into two clocks
u_move_gen/moversthe backward attacksgive G_STAGE a second clock
attackedthe full attack mapregister side_attacks(child, ...) first, then AND it a clock later
childapply_decodedduplicate the decoded registers to cut fanout
u_evalthe addersalready pipelined: check the clock setting first

Each fix adds a clock to one state. That changes clocks per node, but never nodes, scores or moves, so tb_search must still pass afterwards. Vivado's effort settings can also help: Settings, Synthesis, strategy Flow_PerfOptimized_high, and Settings, Implementation, strategy Performance_Explore.

Write the bitstream

  1. Click Generate Bitstream.
  2. Find the two output files (<proj> is C:\chess\vivado\chess_pynq):
    FileWhere
    Bitstream<proj>\chess_pynq.runs\impl_1\system_wrapper.bit
    Hardware handoff<proj>\chess_pynq.gen\sources_1\bd\system\hw_handoff\system.hwh (older Vivado: under chess_pynq.srcs)
  3. For Vitis, export the hardware: File, Export, Export Hardware, choose Include bitstream, and save as C:\chess\output\chess.xsa.

The same thing, by script

Once you have clicked through it once, this script does Steps 34 to 37 in one command, and copies the results and reports to output\:

Create scripts/build.tcl
# build.tcl - creates the whole Vivado project and bitstream without clicking.
# Usage, from the project folder:   vivado -mode batch -source scripts/build.tcl
set clock_mhz 50

set root [file normalize [file join [file dirname [info script]] ..]]
create_project chess_pynq [file join $root vivado] -part xc7z020clg400-1 -force

set boards [get_board_parts -quiet *pynq-z2*]
if {[llength $boards] == 0} {
    error "PYNQ-Z2 board files are not installed: see the board-file step in the guide"
}
set_property board_part [lindex $boards end] [current_project]

add_files -norecurse [glob [file join $root rtl *.sv]]
add_files -norecurse [file join $root rtl chess_axi_top.v]
update_compile_order -fileset sources_1

create_bd_design system
create_bd_cell -type ip -vlnv xilinx.com:ip:processing_system7:5.5 processing_system7_0
apply_bd_automation -rule xilinx.com:bd_rule:processing_system7 \
    -config {make_external "FIXED_IO, DDR" apply_board_preset "1" Master "Disable" Slave "Disable"} \
    [get_bd_cells processing_system7_0]
set_property CONFIG.PCW_FPGA0_PERIPHERAL_FREQMHZ $clock_mhz [get_bd_cells processing_system7_0]

create_bd_cell -type module -reference chess_axi_top chess_axi_top_0
apply_bd_automation -rule xilinx.com:bd_rule:axi4 \
    -config {Clk_master {Auto} Clk_slave {Auto} Clk_xbar {Auto} \
             Master {/processing_system7_0/M_AXI_GP0} Slave {/chess_axi_top_0/s_axi} \
             ddr_seg {Auto} intc_ip {New AXI Interconnect} master_apm {0}} \
    [get_bd_intf_pins chess_axi_top_0/s_axi]
assign_bd_address
validate_bd_design
save_bd_design

add_files -norecurse [make_wrapper -files [get_files system.bd] -top]
set_property top system_wrapper [current_fileset]
update_compile_order -fileset sources_1

launch_runs synth_1 -jobs 4
wait_on_run synth_1
launch_runs impl_1 -to_step write_bitstream -jobs 4
wait_on_run impl_1
if {[get_property PROGRESS [get_runs impl_1]] != "100%"} { error "implementation failed" }

open_run impl_1
set out [file join $root output]
file mkdir $out
report_timing_summary -file [file join $out timing.txt]
report_utilization    -file [file join $out utilization.txt]
write_hw_platform -fixed -include_bit -force -file [file join $out chess.xsa]
file copy -force [glob [file join $root vivado chess_pynq.runs impl_1 *.bit]] [file join $out chess.bit]
file copy -force [file join $root vivado chess_pynq.gen sources_1 bd system hw_handoff system.hwh] \
                 [file join $out chess.hwh]
puts "Bitstream, hardware handoff and reports are in $out"
puts "Worst setup slack: [get_property SLACK [get_timing_paths -delay_type max]] ns"
Command Prompt
cd /d C:\chess
vivado -mode batch -source scripts/build.tcl

Read the last line it prints, and output\timing.txt. Change clock_mhz at the top to try a faster clock.

38First run, with PYNQ and Python

This is the quickest way to see your core work, because it needs no Vitis at all.

Prepare the board

  1. Write the PYNQ-Z2 image to a micro-SD card (images at pynq.io/boards).
  2. Following the PYNQ-Z2 setup guide, set the Boot jumper to SD and the Power jumper to USB.
  3. Connect USB to the PROG-UART port and Ethernet to your PC or network, and switch on.
  4. On a direct cable, the board is at 192.168.2.99; give your PC a fixed address on the same subnet, such as 192.168.2.1. On a network with DHCP it takes an assigned address.

Copy the files

In File Explorer's address bar, type \\192.168.2.99\xilinx (login xilinx, password xilinx), and create a folder named chess. Copy these into it, renaming the first two so they share a base name. The PYNQ documentation requires the .hwh to match the .bit:

FromTo
system_wrapper.bitchess\chess.bit
system.hwhchess\chess.hwh
C:\chess\sw\chess_pynq.pychess\chess_pynq.py

Here is that driver. It reads a FEN, writes the 26 registers, starts a search and reads the result. It is the Python twin of the C driver in the next step.

Create sw/chess_pynq.py
# chess_pynq.py - run the chess core from Jupyter on the PYNQ-Z2.
from pynq import Overlay, MMIO

REG_ID, REG_CONTROL, REG_STATUS, REG_DEPTH = 0x00, 0x04, 0x08, 0x0C
REG_MODE, REG_NODE_LIMIT, REG_META, REG_BEST_MOVE = 0x10, 0x14, 0x18, 0x1C
REG_SCORE, REG_NODES_LO, REG_NODES_HI = 0x20, 0x24, 0x28
REG_CYCLES_LO, REG_CYCLES_HI, REG_BOARDS = 0x2C, 0x30, 0x40
STAT_DONE, STAT_ABORTED, STAT_FAULT = 2, 4, 8
EXPECTED_ID = 0xC4E55A01
PIECES = "PNBRQKpnbrqk"


def parse_fen(fen):
    """Returns (boards, side, castle, ep) in the format the hardware expects."""
    fields = fen.split()
    boards = [0] * 12
    rank, file = 7, 0
    for ch in fields[0]:
        if ch == "/":
            rank, file = rank - 1, 0
        elif ch.isdigit():
            file += int(ch)
        else:
            boards[PIECES.index(ch)] |= 1 << (rank * 8 + file)
            file += 1
    side = 0 if fields[1] == "w" else 1
    castle = sum(bit for ch, bit in zip("KQkq", (1, 2, 4, 8)) if ch in fields[2])
    # A right only counts when the king and rook are really at home.
    if not boards[5] >> 4 & 1:
        castle &= ~3
    if not boards[11] >> 60 & 1:
        castle &= ~12
    if not boards[3] >> 7 & 1:
        castle &= ~1
    if not boards[3] >> 0 & 1:
        castle &= ~2
    if not boards[9] >> 63 & 1:
        castle &= ~4
    if not boards[9] >> 56 & 1:
        castle &= ~8
    ep = 64
    if fields[3] != "-":
        ep = (int(fields[3][1]) - 1) * 8 + "abcdefgh".index(fields[3][0])
    return boards, side, castle, ep


def move_text(word):
    """15-bit hardware move -> text such as e2e4 or a7a8q. 0 means no move."""
    if word == 0:
        return "none"
    frm, to, promo = word & 63, (word >> 6) & 63, (word >> 12) & 7
    text = "abcdefgh"[frm & 7] + str((frm >> 3) + 1)
    text += "abcdefgh"[to & 7] + str((to >> 3) + 1)
    return text + " nbrq"[promo].strip()


class ChessCore:
    def __init__(self, mmio):
        self.mmio = mmio
        found = mmio.read(REG_ID)
        if found != EXPECTED_ID:
            raise RuntimeError(f"ID register reads {found:08x}: wrong bitstream or address")

    def load_fen(self, fen):
        boards, side, castle, ep = parse_fen(fen)
        for i, board in enumerate(boards):
            self.mmio.write(REG_BOARDS + 8 * i, board & 0xFFFFFFFF)
            self.mmio.write(REG_BOARDS + 8 * i + 4, board >> 32)
        self.mmio.write(REG_META, side | (castle << 1) | (ep << 5))

    def run(self, depth, perft=False, node_limit=0):
        self.mmio.write(REG_DEPTH, depth)
        self.mmio.write(REG_MODE, 1 if perft else 0)
        self.mmio.write(REG_NODE_LIMIT, node_limit)
        self.mmio.write(REG_CONTROL, 1)
        while not self.mmio.read(REG_STATUS) & STAT_DONE:
            pass
        status = self.mmio.read(REG_STATUS)
        score = self.mmio.read(REG_SCORE)
        return {
            "best": move_text(self.mmio.read(REG_BEST_MOVE)),
            "score": score - (1 << 32) if score >= (1 << 31) else score,
            "nodes": self.mmio.read(REG_NODES_LO) | (self.mmio.read(REG_NODES_HI) << 32),
            "cycles": self.mmio.read(REG_CYCLES_LO) | (self.mmio.read(REG_CYCLES_HI) << 32),
            "aborted": bool(status & STAT_ABORTED),
            "fault": bool(status & STAT_FAULT),
        }


def open_core(bitfile="chess.bit", base_address=0x43C00000):
    Overlay(bitfile)                    # loads chess.bit and sets the PL clock from chess.hwh
    return ChessCore(MMIO(base_address, 0x1000))

Run it

Open Jupyter in a browser. Current PYNQ images serve it on port 9090: http://192.168.2.99:9090, password xilinx. Open the chess folder and start a new Python 3 notebook there. First cell, with the address you wrote down in Step 35:

Jupyter cell
from chess_pynq import open_core, move_text
core = open_core("chess.bit", base_address=0x43C00000)
print("Core found")

You should see Core found. ID register reads ... means the address or the bitstream is wrong. Next, perft: the most important test on the board.

Jupyter cell
START = "rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1"
KIWI = "r3k2r/p1ppqpb1/bn2pnp1/3PN3/1p2P3/2N2Q1p/PPPBBPPP/R3K2R w KQkq - 0 1"

core.load_fen(START)
r = core.run(4, perft=True)
print(r["nodes"], r["cycles"], "expected 197281 3186591")

core.load_fen(KIWI)
r = core.run(3, perft=True)
print(r["nodes"], r["cycles"], "expected 97862 1432430")

Both the counts and the clock counts must match exactly: the core is fully deterministic, and its clock count doesn't depend on the clock speed. Now a search:

Jupyter cell
core.load_fen(START)
for depth in range(1, 7):
    r = core.run(depth)
    print(depth, r["best"], r["score"], r["nodes"], r["cycles"])

Expected, from running this exact driver code against the simulated hardware:

Expected output
1 b1c3 40 21 489
2 b1c3 10 238 7115
3 b1c3 40 2639 76208
4 b1c3 10 25933 844430
5 d2d4 30 199412 6684151
6 d2d4 10 1519394 55995067

At 50 MHz, 55,995,067 clocks is 1.12 seconds for 1.5 million nodes. The C engine on a desktop took about 3 seconds for the same search. Finally, three special positions:

Jupyter cell
tests = [
    ("mate in one", "6k1/5ppp/8/8/8/8/5PPP/3R2K1 w - - 0 1", 2),  # d1d8, 29999
    ("stalemate",   "7k/5Q2/6K1/8/8/8/8/8 b - - 0 1", 3),         # none, 0
    ("promotion",   "4k3/P7/8/8/8/8/8/4K3 w - - 0 1", 1),         # a7a8q, 890
]
for name, fen, depth in tests:
    core.load_fen(fen)
    r = core.run(depth)
    print(name, r["best"], r["score"])

If all of that matches, your chess engine is running in the programmable logic.

39Bare-metal C, with Vitis

Goal: drive the core from C on the Cortex-A9: the route to your final game.

Concept: the board over AXI4-Lite, end to end

This is the whole conversation between the Cortex-A9 and the chess core. There is no special protocol and no interrupt: the CPU sends a position by writing registers, presses START, watches STATUS, and reads the answer. Every step is one 32-bit load or store to an address between 0x43C0_0000 and 0x43C0_009C.

  1. Check the core is there. Read ID (offset 0x00). It must be 0xC4E55A01. Anything else means the bitstream isn't loaded or the address is wrong, and no other step will work.
  2. Send the twelve bitboards. Each 64-bit board is split into two 32-bit words, low half first: board 0 low at 0x40, board 0 high at 0x44, board 1 low at 0x48, and so on up to board 11 high at 0x9C. That is 24 writes. Write all of them every time, even the zeros, because the shadow registers still hold the previous position.
  3. Send META (0x18): side to move in bit 0, castling rights in bits 4 to 1, en-passant square in bits 11 to 5 (64 for none).
  4. Set the search: DEPTH (0x0C), MODE (0x10, 0 for a search) and NODE_LIMIT (0x14, 0 for none). These keep their values between searches, but writing them each time keeps the code obviously correct.
  5. Write 1 to CONTROL (0x04). In that clock, the core copies the shadow registers into itself and STATUS shows BUSY.
  6. Poll STATUS (0x08) until bit 1, DONE, is set. Your main loop can do other work between polls; a search takes from microseconds to seconds, depending on the depth.
  7. Read the result: BEST_MOVE (0x1C), SCORE (0x20), and if you want them, NODES and CYCLES. If STATUS bit 2, ABORTED, is set, the result is incomplete and must be ignored.

Twenty-eight writes and a handful of reads take a few microseconds on the Zynq's GP0 port, nothing next to the search. Step through it here, for real positions. The values in the table are exactly what pl_write_position sends:

MistakeWhat you seeWhy
Writing the high word first, or swapping low and highpieces on the wrong half of the board; nonsense movesword 2i is bits 31..0, word 2i+1 bits 63..32
Skipping boards that are zeropieces from the previous position appearthe shadow registers keep old values until overwritten
Writing the position while BUSYthe search ignores it and plays a move for the old positionwrites are ignored while a search runs; wait for DONE or ABORT first
Reading BEST_MOVE before DONEthe move from the previous searchresults only change when a search finishes
Using 8- or 16-bit storesgarbled registersthe block ignores wstrb; always use Xil_Out32

Where does the address come from? Vivado's Address Editor (Step 35). Vitis also writes the addresses of the blocks it knows about into xparameters.h; open it and search for 43C0 to see if your core got a name there. The driver uses CHESS_BASE, which defaults to 0x43C00000 and can be overridden with a compiler symbol.

Try it by hand first: the XSCT console

Before writing any C, you can send a position and read the move yourself, one register at a time. This is the best possible test of the AXI-Lite path: if these commands work, the block design, the address and the bitstream are all right, and any later problem is in software. Vitis includes a Tcl console for the debugger, called XSCT (Vitis Classic: Xilinx, XSCT Console) or XSDB (Unified IDE: Vitis, XSDB Console, or run xsdb from a Vivado/Vitis command prompt). Two commands do all the work: mwr address value writes a 32-bit word, and mrd address reads one.

Option A, quickest. Run any application once from Vitis (even an empty "Hello World"), with Program FPGA and Run ps7_init enabled. The logic is now programmed and the processor initialised. In the console:

Tcl console
connect
targets -set -nocase -filter {name =~ "*A9*#0"}
mrd 0x43C00000
Expected output
43C00000:   C4E55A01

Option B, no application at all. An .xsa file is a ZIP archive. Copy C:\chess\output\chess.xsa to chess.zip and extract it to C:\chess\output\hw: inside are the bitstream and ps7_init.tcl, the script that sets up the processor's clocks and DDR. Then this program does everything a C driver does: it loads the bitstream, initialises the processor, writes the starting position into the 24 board registers and META, starts a depth-4 search, waits for DONE and decodes the answer. Save it as C:\chess\scripts\by_hand.tcl, then type source C:/chess/scripts/by_hand.tcl in the console (use forward slashes, and your own bitstream file name).

Tcl console
# by_hand.tcl - send a position over AXI4-Lite and read the best move,
# with no C program. Every line is one 32-bit read or write.
connect
targets -set -nocase -filter {name =~ "APU*"}
rst -system                                  ;# reset the whole Zynq
after 2000
targets -set -nocase -filter {name =~ "xc7z020"}
fpga -file C:/chess/output/hw/system_wrapper.bit   ;# program the logic
targets -set -nocase -filter {name =~ "APU*"}
source C:/chess/output/hw/ps7_init.tcl
ps7_init                                     ;# clocks, DDR, MIO (UART)
ps7_post_config                              ;# enable the PS-to-PL level shifters
targets -set -nocase -filter {name =~ "*A9*#0"}

set BASE 0x43C00000
proc wr {off val} { global BASE; mwr [expr {$BASE + $off}] $val }
proc rd {off} { global BASE; return [lindex [mrd -value [expr {$BASE + $off}]] 0] }

# 1. Is the core there?
puts [format "ID        = 0x%08X (want 0xC4E55A01)" [rd 0x00]]

# 2. The start position: 12 boards x (low word, high word), from 0x40 to 0x9C.
#    White: pawns FF00, knights 42, bishops 24, rooks 81, queen 08, king 10.
#    Black: the same pieces, in the high words (ranks 5 to 8).
set words {0x0000FF00 0  0x42 0  0x24 0  0x81 0  0x08 0  0x10 0
           0 0x00FF0000  0 0x42000000  0 0x24000000  0 0x81000000  0 0x08000000  0 0x10000000}
for {set i 0} {$i < 24} {incr i} { wr [expr {0x40 + 4 * $i}] [lindex $words $i] }

# 3. META = side (0, White) | castling 1111 << 1 | en passant 64 << 5 = 0x81E
wr 0x18 0x81E
# 4. Depth 4, search mode, no node limit, then START.
wr 0x0C 4
wr 0x10 0
wr 0x14 0
wr 0x04 1

# 5. Wait for STATUS bit 1 (DONE).
while {([rd 0x08] & 2) == 0} { after 10 }

# 6. Read and decode the answer.
set m [rd 0x1C]
set f "abcdefgh"
set from [expr {$m & 63}]
set to   [expr {($m >> 6) & 63}]
set score [rd 0x20]
if {$score > 0x7FFFFFFF} { set score [expr {$score - 0x100000000}] }
puts [format "BEST_MOVE = 0x%X = %s%d%s%d" $m [string index $f [expr {$from & 7}]] [expr {($from >> 3) + 1}] \
                                           [string index $f [expr {$to & 7}]]   [expr {($to >> 3) + 1}]]
puts "SCORE     = $score"
puts "NODES     = [rd 0x24]"
puts "CYCLES    = [rd 0x2C]"

Expected output. These numbers come from making exactly these register accesses to the simulated core; the hardware must give the same move, score, node count and clock count:

Expected output
ID        = 0xC4E55A01 (want 0xC4E55A01)
BEST_MOVE = 0x481 = b1c3
SCORE     = 10
NODES     = 25933
CYCLES    = 844430

Read the move word yourself to check you understand it: 0x481 is binary 000 010010 000001. The low six bits are 1, square b1; the next six are 18, square c3; the top three are 0, no promotion. 844,430 clocks at 50 MHz is 17 ms for 25,933 positions.

What you seeMeaningFix
mrd prints an error such as "Memory read error" or "AXI slave error"nothing answers at that address, or the logic is not programmedcheck the Address Editor; run fpga and ps7_post_config again
ID reads 00000000 or a fixed patterna different block is at that addresscheck the Address Editor
The console hangs on the first mrdthe PL clock or the level shifters are offyou skipped ps7_init or ps7_post_config; FCLK_CLK0 must be enabled in the Zynq block
ID is right, STATUS never shows DONESTART was not seenread STATUS: if BUSY is 0 and DONE 0, re-write CONTROL with 1
A different movea board word is wrong or in the wrong orderread back META (rd 0x18) and compare every word with the list above
Code

The driver is a small header. First the register map and two functions that every other function uses: Xil_Out32 and Xil_In32, from the Xilinx board support package, write and read one 32-bit register.

Create sw/chess_pl.hpart 1 of 3
/* chess_pl.h - Cortex-A9 driver for the chess core (bare-metal, Vitis).
 * Everything here is reads and writes of 32-bit registers. */
#ifndef CHESS_PL_H
#define CHESS_PL_H

#include "xil_io.h"       /* Xil_In32, Xil_Out32          */
#include "xtime_l.h"      /* XTime_GetTime, COUNTS_PER_SECOND */
#include "chess.h"

/* The address from Vivado's Address Editor (also in xparameters.h). */
#ifndef CHESS_BASE
#define CHESS_BASE 0x43C00000U
#endif

#define REG_ID          0x00
#define REG_CONTROL     0x04
#define REG_STATUS      0x08
#define REG_DEPTH       0x0C
#define REG_MODE        0x10
#define REG_NODE_LIMIT  0x14
#define REG_META        0x18
#define REG_BEST_MOVE   0x1C
#define REG_SCORE       0x20
#define REG_NODES_LO    0x24
#define REG_CYCLES_LO   0x2C
#define REG_BOARDS      0x40

#define CTRL_START    1u
#define CTRL_ABORT    2u
#define STAT_BUSY     1u
#define STAT_DONE     2u
#define STAT_ABORTED  4u
#define STAT_FAULT    8u
#define CHESS_ID      0xC4E55A01u

static inline void pl_write(uint32_t offset, uint32_t value) {
    Xil_Out32(CHESS_BASE + offset, value);
}
static inline uint32_t pl_read(uint32_t offset) {
    return Xil_In32(CHESS_BASE + offset);
}
static inline uint64_t pl_read64(uint32_t lo_offset) {
    uint32_t lo = pl_read(lo_offset);
    return ((uint64_t)pl_read(lo_offset + 4) << 32) | lo;
}

/* 1 when the bitstream is loaded and the core answers at CHESS_BASE. */
static inline int pl_present(void) {
    return pl_read(REG_ID) == CHESS_ID;
}

Line by line

  1. xil_io.h comes with the Vitis board support package. Xil_Out32(addr, v) is a 32-bit store and Xil_In32(addr) a 32-bit load, through a volatile pointer, so the compiler can never remove, merge or reorder them. The standalone BSP maps the PL address range as device memory, so the processor sends them to the bus in program order too.
  2. CHESS_BASE is wrapped in #ifndef, so you can change it with a compiler symbol (-DCHESS_BASE=...) without editing the file.
  3. The REG_ offsets are byte offsets, exactly the ones in the register map of Step 32. The CTRL_ and STAT_ values are bit masks for CONTROL and STATUS.
  4. pl_read64 reads a 48-bit counter as two words, low first. The counters only change while the core is busy, and we read them after DONE, so the two halves always belong together.
  5. pl_present is the first thing any program should call: if the ID register is wrong, nothing else will work.

Writing a position is 24 board words plus one META word; then pl_start sets the depth and mode and writes START. pl_run waits for DONE and collects the results.

Add to sw/chess_pl.hpart 2 of 3
/* Send a position: 24 board words, then META. Board i is split in two:
 *   0x40 + 8*i  <- bits 31..0  (squares a1..h4)
 *   0x44 + 8*i  <- bits 63..32 (squares a5..h8)
 * All 24 are written every time, even zeros, so nothing is left over from
 * the previous position. The core ignores these writes while it is busy. */
static inline void pl_write_position(const Position *p) {
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < 12; i++) {
        pl_write(REG_BOARDS + 8 * i,     (uint32_t)p->bb[i]);           /* low  */
        pl_write(REG_BOARDS + 8 * i + 4, (uint32_t)(p->bb[i] >> 32));   /* high */
    }
    pl_write(REG_META, (uint32_t)p->side                 /* bit 0          */
                     | ((uint32_t)p->castle << 1)        /* bits 4..1      */
                     | ((uint32_t)p->ep << 5));          /* bits 11..5     */
}

/* Start one search (perft_mode = 0) or perft (perft_mode = 1). Writing
 * START copies the whole shadow position into the core in one clock. */
static inline void pl_start(int depth, int perft_mode, uint32_t node_limit) {
    pl_write(REG_DEPTH, (uint32_t)depth);
    pl_write(REG_MODE, perft_mode ? 1u : 0u);
    pl_write(REG_NODE_LIMIT, node_limit);
    pl_write(REG_CONTROL, CTRL_START);
}

static inline int  pl_done(void)  { return (pl_read(REG_STATUS) & STAT_DONE) != 0; }
static inline void pl_abort(void) { pl_write(REG_CONTROL, CTRL_ABORT); }

typedef struct {
    Move     best;
    int      score;
    uint64_t nodes;
    uint64_t cycles;
    int      depth;      /* deepest iteration that finished */
} PlResult;

/* Run one search or perft and wait for it: send, start, poll, read.
 * This blocks; a game should use the Thinker below instead. */
static inline PlResult pl_run(const Position *p, int depth, int perft_mode) {
    PlResult r;
    pl_write_position(p);
    pl_start(depth, perft_mode, 0);
    while (!pl_done()) { }
    r.best   = (Move)pl_read(REG_BEST_MOVE);
    r.score  = (int32_t)pl_read(REG_SCORE);
    r.nodes  = pl_read64(REG_NODES_LO);
    r.cycles = pl_read64(REG_CYCLES_LO);
    r.depth  = depth;
    return r;
}

Line by line

  1. pl_write_position is the "transmit the board" function. The loop sends board i as two writes at 0x40 + 8i (low word, (uint32_t)bb keeps bits 31..0) and 0x44 + 8i (high word, bb >> 32).
  2. The META word is assembled with shifts and ORs to match the bit layout the RTL slices apart: side | castle << 1 | ep << 5.
  3. pl_start writes the three settings, then CONTROL = START. The order matters: START must be the last write, because the core takes its snapshot on that clock.
  4. pl_run (the rest of this snippet) is the blocking version: start, spin on pl_done(), then collect everything into a PlResult. It is ideal for tests; a game uses the non-blocking thinker below instead.

A game needs a time limit, and it must keep drawing the screen while the engine thinks. Thinker does iterative deepening: search depth 1, then 2, then 3, keeping the last finished answer, until the time budget runs out. Then it sends ABORT. The aborted search is thrown away, so the answer is always from a complete search. It never blocks: your main loop calls think_poll as often as it likes.

Add to sw/chess_pl.hpart 3 of 3
/* Iterative deepening under a time budget, without blocking: call
 * think_begin once, then think_poll from your main loop until it returns 1.
 * The answer always comes from the last iteration that finished. */
typedef struct {
    XTime    t0;
    uint64_t budget_ticks;
    int      max_depth, depth, abort_sent;
    PlResult result;
} Thinker;

static inline void think_begin(Thinker *t, const Position *p, int max_depth,
                               uint32_t budget_ms) {
    XTime_GetTime(&t->t0);
    t->budget_ticks = (uint64_t)COUNTS_PER_SECOND * budget_ms / 1000;
    t->max_depth = max_depth;
    t->depth = 1;
    t->abort_sent = 0;
    memset(&t->result, 0, sizeof t->result);
    pl_write_position(p);
    pl_start(t->depth, 0, 0);
}

static inline int think_poll(Thinker *t, PlResult *out) {
    if (!pl_done()) {                         /* still searching */
        XTime now;
        XTime_GetTime(&now);
        if (!t->abort_sent && (uint64_t)(now - t->t0) > t->budget_ticks) {
            pl_abort();                       /* out of time */
            t->abort_sent = 1;
        }
        return 0;
    }
    if (!(pl_read(REG_STATUS) & STAT_ABORTED)) {   /* this depth finished */
        int forced;
        t->result.best    = (Move)pl_read(REG_BEST_MOVE);
        t->result.score   = (int32_t)pl_read(REG_SCORE);
        t->result.nodes  += pl_read64(REG_NODES_LO);
        t->result.cycles += pl_read64(REG_CYCLES_LO);
        t->result.depth   = t->depth;
        forced = t->result.best == 0 || t->result.score >= MATE - MAX_PLY;
        if (t->depth < t->max_depth && !forced && !t->abort_sent) {
            pl_start(++t->depth, 0, 0);       /* go one ply deeper */
            return 0;
        }
    }
    *out = t->result;
    return 1;
}

#endif

Line by line

  1. think_begin notes the start time with the A9's global timer (XTime_GetTime, which counts at COUNTS_PER_SECOND), converts the budget from milliseconds to timer ticks, sends the position, and starts depth 1.
  2. think_poll first asks "is the core done?". If not, it checks the clock, and once the budget is used it sends ABORT exactly once (abort_sent), then returns 0: "not yet".
  3. When the core is done and was not aborted, this depth finished. Its move and score become the current answer, and the node and clock counts are added up.
  4. If there is depth left, time left, and the score is not already a forced mate, it starts the next depth with pl_start alone: the position is still in the shadow registers, so it does not need to be sent again.
  5. Otherwise, or if the last search was aborted, it returns 1 and the result of the deepest search that finished. An aborted search is never used: its move could be a half-examined mistake.

The bring-up program checks the ID, runs both perfts, searches depths 1 to 6, then thinks for one second, printing everything on the serial port:

Create sw/main_baremetal.c
/* main_baremetal.c - bring-up test on the Cortex-A9. Prints on the UART. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include "chess_pl.h"

static int check_perft(const char *name, const char *fen, int depth, uint64_t expected) {
    Position p;
    PlResult r;
    from_fen(fen, &p);
    r = pl_run(&p, depth, 1);
    printf("perft %-8s depth %d: %llu (expected %llu) %s, %llu clocks\r\n",
           name, depth, (unsigned long long)r.nodes, (unsigned long long)expected,
           r.nodes == expected ? "OK" : "FAIL", (unsigned long long)r.cycles);
    return r.nodes == expected;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *start_fen = "rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1";
    const char *kiwipete  = "r3k2r/p1ppqpb1/bn2pnp1/3PN3/1p2P3/2N2Q1p/PPPBBPPP/R3K2R w KQkq - 0 1";
    static Thinker thinker;
    Position p;
    PlResult r;
    char text[6];
    int ok, d;

    printf("\r\nchess core bring-up\r\n");
    if (!pl_present()) {
        printf("FAIL: ID register reads %08lx\r\n", (unsigned long)pl_read(REG_ID));
        return 1;
    }
    printf("ID register OK\r\n");

    ok = check_perft("start", start_fen, 4, 197281);
    ok = check_perft("kiwipete", kiwipete, 3, 97862) && ok;
    if (!ok) {
        printf("PERFT FAILED: do not trust searches\r\n");
        return 1;
    }

    from_fen(start_fen, &p);
    for (d = 1; d <= 6; d++) {
        r = pl_run(&p, d, 0);
        move_to_text(r.best, text);
        printf("depth %d best %s score %d nodes %llu clocks %llu (%llu clocks/node)\r\n",
               d, text, r.score, (unsigned long long)r.nodes,
               (unsigned long long)r.cycles, (unsigned long long)(r.cycles / r.nodes));
    }

    think_begin(&thinker, &p, 20, 1000);
    while (!think_poll(&thinker, &r)) {
        /* your VGA and controller code keeps running here */
    }
    move_to_text(r.best, text);
    printf("1 second think: best %s score %d depth %d nodes %llu\r\n",
           text, r.score, r.depth, (unsigned long long)r.nodes);
    printf("DONE\r\n");
    return 0;
}

Prepare the board

  1. Set the Boot jumper to JTAG. Connect USB to PROG-UART and switch on.
  2. In Windows Device Manager, under Ports, find the board's COM port. Open it in PuTTY or Tera Term at 115200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit.

Create the application

Vitis Classic (2023.1 and earlier):

  1. Start Vitis with a workspace such as C:\chess\vitis.
  2. File, New, Application Project, Next.
  3. Create a new platform from hardware (XSA): browse to C:\chess\output\chess.xsa, Next.
  4. Name the application chess_test, processor ps7_cortexa9_0, Next. Keep the standalone domain, Next.
  5. Choose Empty Application (C), Finish.

Vitis Unified IDE (2023.2 and later):

  1. File, New Component, Platform. Name it chess_platform, choose your .xsa, operating system standalone, processor ps7_cortexa9_0. Build it from the Flow panel.
  2. File, New Component, Application. Name it chess_test and select the platform and its domain.

Add the code and run

  1. Copy c\chess.h, sw\chess_pl.h, sw\game.h and sw\main_baremetal.c into the application's src folder.
  2. If your Address Editor showed a different address, add -DCHESS_BASE=0x... to the compiler's other flags (Classic: right-click the application, C/C++ Build Settings, ARM v7 gcc compiler, Miscellaneous).
  3. Build the application.
  4. Run it. Classic: right-click the application, Run As, Launch Hardware. Unified: Run in the Flow panel. Make sure Program FPGA and Run ps7_init are enabled; they normally are for an XSA with a bitstream.

40Look inside the chip with an ILA

You should rarely need this, because simulation found the logic bugs. If the board disagrees with simulation, an Integrated Logic Analyzer (ILA) records real signals inside the running chip.

  1. Mark the signals you want in search_core.sv, for example:
    SystemVerilog
    (* mark_debug = "true" *) state_t state;
(* mark_debug = "true" *) logic [4:0] ply;
(* mark_debug = "true" *) move_t move_r;
(* mark_debug = "true" *) logic signed [15:0] ret;
  2. Run synthesis and open the synthesized design. Choose Tools, Set Up Debug, Next. The marked nets are listed; pick the FCLK clock domain if asked, a sample depth such as 4096, and Finish.
  3. Save (Ctrl+S), then Generate Bitstream.
  4. With the board in JTAG mode, open Open Hardware Manager, Open Target, Auto Connect, then Program Device with the .bit and the .ltx probes file beside it.
  5. Start your program from Vitis with Program FPGA turned off, so it doesn't reload a bitstream. In the ILA window, set a trigger such as state == S_POP and click Run.

What to look for

  • Trigger on state leaving S_IDLE to catch the start of a search. The next few hundred samples should walk through S_ENTER, S_CLASSIFY, the generator wait and S_NEXT, just as in the trace figure of Step 31.
  • If state never leaves S_IDLE, START never arrived: look at the AXI side instead (s_axi_awvalid, s_axi_wvalid, s_axi_bvalid).
  • If ply climbs to 31 and stays there, the search is not returning: compare with the same position in simulation.
  • If the core finishes but the move differs from simulation, capture move_r at the root (ply == 0) and compare the sequence of moves tried with the C engine's move list for the same position.

Probing all 780 bits of a position is rarely useful. Start with the small signals.

Part 4

The playable game: UART in, VGA out

Part 3 proved the core on its own. Now it joins your GPU in one design, and the Cortex-A9 becomes the referee: it reads your moves from a serial terminal, checks them, draws the board with your samGL library, and hands the thinking to the hardware. Each step below ends with something you can check, and every program in this part was run, unchanged, against the simulated chess core plus models of your GPU and the UART.

41The plan: who does what

Goal: know exactly which part of the chip owns which job before writing any code.

Concept

Three workers share the board, and each does only what it is best at:

  • The chess core (PL) only searches. It gets a position, finds the best move, and says how good it thinks the position is. It knows nothing about the game's history, the screen, or you.
  • Your GPU (PL) only draws: a pixel, or a filled rectangle, into a 320 × 240 frame that it sends to the VGA monitor.
  • The Cortex-A9 (PS) runs the game. It reads keys from the UART, turns e2e4 into a move, checks the move is legal, keeps the history for repetitions and undo, decides what to draw, and starts and stops the chess core's searches.

Here is the finished game, running in this page. It uses a JavaScript copy of the renderer you are about to write, drawing your own sprites into a 320 × 240 frame with your palette, and the same commands as the C program. Type e2e4 and press Enter.

One turn, step by step

  1. You type e2e4 and Enter in the terminal. Each key travels as one byte over the USB cable into the PS UART's receive FIFO.
  2. The main loop polls the UART. The line is complete, so it parses it into a move and checks it against the legal moves.
  3. The move is played on the Game. The renderer redraws only the four squares that changed.
  4. Now it is the engine's turn. The A9 writes the position into the core and presses START. The lamp turns red.
  5. While the core searches, the loop keeps running: it fills the thinking bar and would still read keys. Each time a depth finishes, the thinker starts the next one, until the time is up.
  6. The A9 reads the best move, plays it, redraws, updates the evaluation bar, and prints the move. Your turn again.

The files

FileFromJob
chess.hPart 1the rules: move generation, legality, FEN
chess_pl.hStep 39talks to the chess core over AXI, and the Thinker
game.hStep 47a game: history, legality of your moves, game over
samgl.h, sprites.hyour codeyour GPU library and your piece sprites

render.hSteps 45 and 46draws the board, the bars and the lamp
main_game.cStep 47the game loop and the commands

42Put your GPU and the chess core in one design

Goal: one bitstream with both blocks, at known addresses, and the serial port enabled.

Concept

The Zynq gives its GP0 master port a 1 GB address window, from 0x4000_0000 to 0x7FFF_FFFF. An AXI interconnect splits that window between the blocks attached to it. Your library expects the GPU at 0x4000_0000 (or wherever XPAR_GPU_BASEADDR says), and the chess driver expects 0x43C0_0000. Each block gets a 4 KB or 64 KB slice; they must not overlap, and the Address Editor guarantees that.

BlockBase addressUsed by
Your GPU0x4000_0000GPU_BASEADDR in samgl.h
Chess core0x43C0_0000CHESS_BASE in chess_pl.h
PS UART00xE000_0000fixed inside the processor; uart_in.h and printf

On the PYNQ-Z2, UART0 is wired through MIO pins 14 and 15 to the same USB chip as the JTAG programmer, so one micro-USB cable programs the board and carries your moves. The board preset turns UART0 on at 115200 baud.

Do it
  1. Open the Vivado project that holds your GPU. (Or open chess_pynq from Step 34 and add your GPU's IP to it; the steps are the same.)
  2. Add the seven chess files: in the Flow Navigator, Add Sources, Add or create design sources, Add Files, select everything in C:\chess\rtl, untick Copy sources into project, Finish.
  3. Open the block design. Right-click an empty area, Add Module, choose chess_axi_top.
  4. Click Run Connection Automation, tick All Automation, OK. Vivado connects s_axi to the existing interconnect (adding a master port to it), and the clock and reset to the same ones your GPU's AXI port uses.
  5. Check the clock on chess_axi_top_0/aclk. If it is FCLK_CLK0 at 50 MHz, you are done. If your design runs the AXI bus faster, either check timing passes for the core at that speed (Step 37), or give the core its own 50 MHz clock with a second interconnect, as Step 35 describes.
  6. Double-click the Zynq block and open Peripheral I/O Pins (in some versions, MIO Configuration, I/O Peripherals). Check that UART 0 is ticked on MIO 14 .. 15. OK.
  7. Open the Address Editor. You should see two rows under processing_system7_0 / Data: your GPU at 0x4000_0000 and chess_axi_top_0 at 0x43C0_0000. If Vivado picked other addresses, either change them here, or remember them for Step 43.
  8. F6 to validate, Ctrl+S, then Generate Bitstream. Check timing as in Step 37.
  9. File, Export, Export Hardware, choose Include bitstream, and save it as C:\chess\output\chess_game.xsa.
Check

The implemented design's utilisation report should show your GPU's resources plus about 11,400 LUTs and 16 block RAMs for the chess core. If the bitstream builds and timing is met, the hardware side is finished: everything from here is C.

43Create the game application in Vitis
