44Read keys from the UART without ever waiting

Goal: collect typed lines while the screen and the engine keep running.

Concept

The obvious way to read a line is scanf or getchar. Both block: the processor sits inside them until you press Enter. While it waits, nothing else in the loop runs: the thinking bar would freeze, and, worse, the A9 could not collect the engine's answer.

So we poll instead. The UART has a 64-byte receive FIFO that fills by itself as bytes arrive, whatever the processor is doing. Each time round the main loop, we look at its status register. If the FIFO is empty we return at once; if not, we take every byte waiting, add it to a line buffer, and report a finished line when we see Enter. A human types perhaps ten keys a second, and the loop runs millions of times a second, so nothing is ever lost.

Only two of the UART's registers are needed. Both names come from xuartps_hw.h, part of Vitis's standalone library:

RegisterOffsetWhat we use
Channel status, XUARTPS_SR_OFFSET0x2Cbit 1, RXEMPTY: 1 while the receive FIFO is empty. XUartPs_IsReceiveData tests it.
FIFO, XUARTPS_FIFO_OFFSET0x30reading takes the oldest received byte
Code
Create sw/uart_in.h
/* uart_in.h - read typed lines from the PS UART without ever waiting.
 * On the PYNQ-Z2, UART0 is wired to the USB serial port (PROG/UART). */
#ifndef UART_IN_H
#define UART_IN_H

#include "xuartps_hw.h"      /* register names and the IsReceiveData macro */
#include "xparameters.h"

#ifndef UART_BASE
#  ifdef STDIN_BASEADDRESS
#    define UART_BASE STDIN_BASEADDRESS   /* the UART printf already uses */
#  else
#    define UART_BASE 0xE0000000u         /* PS UART0 */
#  endif
#endif

#define LINE_MAX 96          /* long enough for "fen" plus a full FEN */

typedef struct {
    char text[LINE_MAX];     /* the finished line, 0-terminated */
    int  len;                /* characters typed so far         */
} LineReader;

/* Take every byte waiting in the receive FIFO. Returns 1 when Enter
 * finishes a line (now in r->text), 0 if the line is not finished yet.
 * Typed characters are echoed, and Backspace works. */
static int uart_poll_line(LineReader *r) {
    while (XUartPs_IsReceiveData(UART_BASE)) {
        char c = (char)XUartPs_ReadReg(UART_BASE, XUARTPS_FIFO_OFFSET);

        if (c == '\r' || c == '\n') {             /* Enter */
            if (r->len == 0) continue;            /* ignore empty lines and \r\n */
            r->text[r->len] = '\0';
            r->len = 0;
            XUartPs_SendByte(UART_BASE, '\r');
            XUartPs_SendByte(UART_BASE, '\n');
            return 1;
        }
        if (c == '\b' || c == 127) {              /* Backspace or Delete */
            if (r->len > 0) {
                r->len--;
                XUartPs_SendByte(UART_BASE, '\b');  /* erase it on screen */
                XUartPs_SendByte(UART_BASE, ' ');
                XUartPs_SendByte(UART_BASE, '\b');
            }
            continue;
        }
        if (c >= ' ' && c <= '~' && r->len < LINE_MAX - 1) {
            r->text[r->len++] = c;
            XUartPs_SendByte(UART_BASE, (u8)c);     /* echo */
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

#endif

Three details. Echo: the terminal does not show what you type unless the board sends it back, so every accepted character is written back with XUartPs_SendByte. Line endings: terminals send Enter as \r, \n or both; the empty-line check swallows the second half of a \r\n pair. Backspace: the "back, space, back" sequence erases the character on screen too.

STDIN_BASEADDRESS is the UART that the BSP connected to printf, so the game's input and output always use the same port.

Line by line: typing e2e4 and Enter

  1. The loop calls uart_poll_line perhaps a million times before you press the first key. Each time, XUartPs_IsReceiveData reads the status register, sees RXEMPTY = 1, and the function returns 0 at once.
  2. You press e. The byte 0x65 arrives over USB and lands in the receive FIFO. On the next call the while condition is true, XUartPs_ReadReg takes the byte, it is printable, so it goes into text[0], len becomes 1, and the byte is echoed. The FIFO is now empty, the while ends, and the function returns 0: the line is not finished.
  3. 2, e, 4 follow the same path. text holds "e2e4", len is 4.
  4. You press Enter. PuTTY sends \r (0x0D). The function writes the terminating \0, resets len to 0 for the next line, moves the cursor to a new line on your screen, and returns 1. The caller now reads line.text.
  5. If your terminal sends \r\n, the \n arrives with len = 0 and is skipped by continue, so one Enter is always one line.
  6. Characters beyond LINE_MAX − 1 are dropped, so a long paste can never overflow the buffer.

45Your library, the layout, and sprites as runs

Goal: draw one piece as fast as your GPU allows, using only your library.

Concept

Your library has two ways to draw. samGL_DrawPixel writes three registers (X, Y, colour) per pixel. samGL_HardwareDrawRect writes six registers (X, Y, width, height, colour, START), and then the GPU fills the whole rectangle by itself. A rectangle costs twice as much as a pixel to start, but any rectangle wider than two pixels is a bargain.

A sprite row is mostly long stretches of one colour: transparent, then outline, then body. So the renderer cuts each row into runs of one colour and draws every visible run as a one-pixel-high rectangle. Transparent runs are simply skipped, so the square's colour shows through.

Your sprites are 16 × 16, drawn at 24 × 24. Your SpriteScaleMap table says which source pixel each screen pixel copies: every second source pixel is used twice, so 16 become 24. This is nearest-neighbour scaling, the same thing a game console does, and it keeps the pixel-art edges sharp.

Code

First, your library, unchanged except that each function is now static inline, so the header can be included safely:

Create sw/samgl.h
/* samgl.h - your GPU library, moved into a header so every file can use it.
 * The only change: each function is "static inline", so including the header in
 * more than one place cannot cause duplicate definitions. */
#ifndef SAMGL_H
#define SAMGL_H
// INTERNAL -----------------
#include <stdio.h>
#include "xil_io.h"
#include "xparameters.h"
#include "sleep.h"

// Base ADD
#ifdef XPAR_GPU_BASEADDR
#define GPU_BASEADDR XPAR_GPU_BASEADDR
#else
#define GPU_BASEADDR 0x40000000
#endif

// AXI
#define REG_GPU_STATUS   0x00
#define REG_PIXEL_X      0x30
#define REG_PIXEL_Y      0x34
#define REG_PIXEL_COLOR  0x38
#define REG_RECT_W       0x3C
#define REG_RECT_H       0x40
#define REG_START        0x44
#define REG_VERSION      0x48
#define GPU_WRITE(offset, data) Xil_Out32(GPU_BASEADDR + (offset), (u32)(data))
#define GPU_READ(offset)        Xil_In32(GPU_BASEADDR + (offset))



#define RGB444(r, g, b) (((r & 0xF) << 8) | ((g & 0xF) << 4) | (b & 0xF))
#define PAL_INDEX(r, g, b) ((((r) / 2) * 32) + (((g) / 2) * 4) + ((b) / 4))
#define SCREEN_W 320
#define SCREEN_H 240


// GPU Library //
static inline void samGL_DrawPixel(u32 x, u32 y, u16 color) {
    if (x >= SCREEN_W || y >= SCREEN_H) return;
    GPU_WRITE(REG_PIXEL_X, x);
    GPU_WRITE(REG_PIXEL_Y, y);
    GPU_WRITE(REG_PIXEL_COLOR, color);
}

static inline void samGL_DrawRect(u32 start_x, u32 start_y, u32 width, u32 height, u16 color) {
    for (u32 y = start_y; y < start_y + height; y++) {
        for (u32 x = start_x; x < start_x + width; x++) {
            samGL_DrawPixel(x, y, color);
        }
    }
}

static inline void samGL_ClearScreen_CPU(u16 color) {
    for (u32 y = 0; y < SCREEN_H; y++) {
        for (u32 x = 0; x < SCREEN_W; x++) {
            samGL_DrawPixel(x, y, color);
        }
    }
}

static inline void samGL_Flush(void) {
    while (GPU_READ(REG_GPU_STATUS) & 0x01) {
        // wait
    }
}

static inline void samGL_HardwareDrawRect(u32 x, u32 y, u32 w, u32 h, u16 color) {
    samGL_Flush();
    GPU_WRITE(REG_PIXEL_X, x);
    GPU_WRITE(REG_PIXEL_Y, y);
    GPU_WRITE(REG_RECT_W, w);
    GPU_WRITE(REG_RECT_H, h);
    GPU_WRITE(REG_PIXEL_COLOR, color);
    GPU_WRITE(REG_START, 1);
}

static inline void samGL_HardwareClearScreen(u16 color) {
    samGL_Flush();
    samGL_HardwareDrawRect(0, 0, SCREEN_W, SCREEN_H, color);
}

static inline void samGL_Init(){
    u32 hw_version = GPU_READ(REG_VERSION);
    printf("\n==========================================\n");
    printf("FPGA GPU Hardware Version: 0x%08X\n", hw_version);
    printf("=-=-BY SWR06-=-=\n");
    printf("==========================================\n\n");
}

#endif

The layout keeps your board exactly where it was (28-pixel squares, centred) and uses the two 48-pixel margins: an evaluation bar on the left, and a lamp and thinking bar on the right. Colours are your palette indexes, made with your PAL_INDEX macro. Its 3-3-2 format has only four levels of blue, so the highlight colours were picked from the strong reds, yellows and greens it can show.

Create sw/render.hpart 1 of 4
/* render.h - draws the game with your samGL library.
 * Two ideas keep it fast: only squares that changed are redrawn, and
 * sprites are drawn as horizontal runs by the rectangle engine. */
#ifndef RENDER_H
#define RENDER_H

#include <string.h>
#include "samgl.h"
#include "sprites.h"
#include "chess.h"

/* Layout on the 320 x 240 screen. The board is centred, as in your code. */
#define SQ_PX     28                              /* one square            */
#define PIECE_PX  24                              /* a 16 px sprite at 1.5x */
#define BOARD_PX  (8 * SQ_PX)                     /* 224                   */
#define BOARD_X   ((SCREEN_W - BOARD_PX) / 2)     /* 48                    */
#define BOARD_Y   ((SCREEN_H - BOARD_PX) / 2)     /* 8                     */
#define FRAME_PX  3
#define EVAL_X    18                              /* evaluation bar, left  */
#define EVAL_W    12
#define SIDE_X    (BOARD_X + BOARD_PX + FRAME_PX + 14)   /* right column  */
#define LAMP_PX   12                              /* whose-turn lamp       */
#define THINK_Y   (BOARD_Y + LAMP_PX + 8)         /* thinking bar          */
#define THINK_W   LAMP_PX
#define THINK_H   (BOARD_Y + BOARD_PX - THINK_Y)

/* Colours, as indexes into your 3-3-2 palette. */
enum {
    COL_BACKGROUND = PAL_INDEX(2, 4, 0),    /* your theme ...          */
    COL_FRAME      = PAL_INDEX(4, 2, 0),
    COL_LIGHT      = PAL_INDEX(14, 12, 8),
    COL_DARK       = PAL_INDEX(10, 6, 4),
    COL_LAST_LIGHT = PAL_INDEX(14, 14, 4),  /* ... plus highlights     */
    COL_LAST_DARK  = PAL_INDEX(12, 10, 0),
    COL_CHECK      = PAL_INDEX(14, 2, 0),
    COL_WHITE      = PAL_INDEX(14, 14, 12),
    COL_BLACK      = PAL_INDEX(0, 0, 0),
    COL_YOUR_TURN  = PAL_INDEX(4, 12, 4),   /* lamp colours            */
    COL_THINKING   = PAL_INDEX(12, 2, 0),
    COL_GAME_OVER  = PAL_INDEX(14, 14, 4),
    COL_THINK_BAR  = PAL_INDEX(6, 10, 14)
};

/* What the screen shows, so we can redraw only what changes.
 * cell[sq] = sprite number + 1 (0 = empty), plus a highlight in bits 4-5. */
enum { MARK_NONE = 0, MARK_LAST = 1, MARK_CHECK = 2 };
#define CELL(sprite1, mark) ((uint8_t)((sprite1) | ((mark) << 4)))
#define CELL_UNKNOWN 0xFF

typedef struct {
    uint8_t cell[64];
    int     flipped;        /* 1 = Black at the bottom              */
    int     think_rows;     /* rows of the thinking bar filled so far */
} Screen;

The Screen struct is the renderer's memory of what the monitor shows right now. One byte per square is enough: which sprite (0 to 12) and which highlight (none, last move, check). Step 46 uses it to skip squares that are already right.

Add to sw/render.hpart 2 of 4
/* Your 1.5x scaling table: destination pixel -> sprite pixel. */
static const u8 SpriteScaleMap[PIECE_PX] = {
    0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7,
    8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 15
};

/* Sprite order is K Q B N R P (black, then white). Engine order is
 * PAWN KNIGHT BISHOP ROOK QUEEN KING, so translate with a table. */
static const u8 SPRITE_OF_TYPE[6] = { 5, 3, 2, 4, 1, 0 };

/* Sprite number + 1 of the piece on sq, or 0 for an empty square. */
static int sprite_on(const Position *p, int sq) {
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < 12; i++)
        if (p->bb[i] & BIT(sq))
            return (i / 6 == WHITE ? 6 : 0) + SPRITE_OF_TYPE[i % 6] + 1;
    return 0;
}

/* Draw one sprite with its top-left corner at (x0, y0). Each row is cut
 * into runs of one colour; every visible run is one hardware rectangle,
 * instead of one AXI write sequence per pixel. */
static void draw_sprite(int sprite, u32 x0, u32 y0) {
    const u16 *pixels = PieceBitmap + sprite * PIECE_SPRITE_PIXELS;
    u32 dy, dx, start;

    for (dy = 0; dy < PIECE_PX; dy++) {
        const u16 *row = pixels + SpriteScaleMap[dy] * PIECE_SPRITE_W;
        for (dx = 0; dx < PIECE_PX; ) {
            u16 colour = row[SpriteScaleMap[dx]];
            start = dx;
            while (dx < PIECE_PX && row[SpriteScaleMap[dx]] == colour) dx++;
            if (colour != SPRITE_TRANSPARENT)
                samGL_HardwareDrawRect(x0 + start, y0 + dy, dx - start, 1, colour);
        }
    }
}

The engine numbers pieces PAWN = 0 to KING = 5; your sprites go king, queen, bishop, knight, rook, pawn. SPRITE_OF_TYPE translates, so neither side has to change. In draw_sprite, the inner while extends a run as long as the next pixel has the same colour; when it stops, dx − start is the run's width.

Why not keep DrawPixel?

It works, and it is what your prototype does. Drawing the 32 pieces of the starting position pixel by pixel takes 25,944 register writes; as runs, 17,856. That saving is real but modest. The next step matters far more: most frames redraw only four squares.

46Redraw only what changed

Goal: update the screen after a move in about a tenth of the work of a full redraw, with no flicker.

Concept

Your prototype clears the screen and redraws everything after each move. On the GPU that is about 18,000 register writes, and for a moment the screen shows an empty board: that is the flicker you may have seen.

Instead, the renderer remembers what each square shows (the Screen struct), works out what each square should show, and redraws only the squares where the two differ. After a normal move that is four squares: the two squares of the new move, which become highlighted, and the two squares of the previous move, which lose their highlight. Castling adds the rook's two squares. A check adds the king's square.

Code
Add to sw/render.hpart 3 of 4
/* Screen position of a square. a1 is bottom-left unless flipped. */
static void square_xy(const Screen *s, int sq, u32 *x, u32 *y) {
    int file = sq & 7, rank = sq >> 3;
    int col = s->flipped ? 7 - file : file;
    int row = s->flipped ? rank : 7 - rank;
    *x = BOARD_X + col * SQ_PX;
    *y = BOARD_Y + row * SQ_PX;
}

static void draw_cell(const Screen *s, int sq, uint8_t cell) {
    int light = ((sq >> 3) + (sq & 7)) & 1;     /* a1 (0 + 0) is dark */
    int mark = cell >> 4, sprite1 = cell & 15;
    u16 colour = light ? COL_LIGHT : COL_DARK;
    u32 x, y;

    if (mark == MARK_LAST)  colour = light ? COL_LAST_LIGHT : COL_LAST_DARK;
    if (mark == MARK_CHECK) colour = COL_CHECK;
    square_xy(s, sq, &x, &y);
    samGL_HardwareDrawRect(x, y, SQ_PX, SQ_PX, colour);
    if (sprite1)
        draw_sprite(sprite1 - 1, x + (SQ_PX - PIECE_PX) / 2, y + (SQ_PX - PIECE_PX) / 2);
}

/* Bring the board up to date with position p. "last" is the move just
 * played (0 for none); its squares are highlighted, and so is a king in
 * check. Returns how many squares had to be redrawn. */
static int render_board(Screen *s, const Position *p, Move last) {
    uint8_t want[64];
    int sq, redrawn = 0;

    for (sq = 0; sq < 64; sq++) want[sq] = CELL(sprite_on(p, sq), MARK_NONE);
    if (last) {
        want[MOVE_FROM(last)] |= MARK_LAST << 4;
        want[MOVE_TO(last)]   |= MARK_LAST << 4;
    }
    if (in_check(p)) {
        sq = lsb(p->bb[p->side * 6 + KING]);
        want[sq] = (uint8_t)((want[sq] & 15) | (MARK_CHECK << 4));
    }
    for (sq = 0; sq < 64; sq++) {
        if (want[sq] != s->cell[sq]) {
            draw_cell(s, sq, want[sq]);
            s->cell[sq] = want[sq];
            redrawn++;
        }
    }
    samGL_Flush();
    return redrawn;
}

render_board is the whole idea in twenty lines. It builds want, compares it with s->cell, and draws the differences. Because it compares the final picture, not the move, it never needs special cases: castling, en passant and promotion all just work. And any time the screen might be wrong, after "new" or "flip", setting every cell to CELL_UNKNOWN forces a full redraw.

Add to sw/render.hpart 4 of 4
/* The lamp above the thinking bar: green = your move, red = thinking. */
static void render_lamp(u16 colour) {
    samGL_HardwareDrawRect(SIDE_X - 1, BOARD_Y - 1, LAMP_PX + 2, LAMP_PX + 2, COL_FRAME);
    samGL_HardwareDrawRect(SIDE_X, BOARD_Y, LAMP_PX, LAMP_PX, colour);
    samGL_Flush();
}

/* Evaluation bar: White's share grows upward from the bottom (from the
 * top when flipped). white_cp is the score from White's view, in
 * centipawns; +/-800 or more fills almost the whole bar. */
static void render_eval(const Screen *s, int white_cp) {
    int lim = 800, white_px;
    if (white_cp > lim) white_cp = lim;
    if (white_cp < -lim) white_cp = -lim;
    white_px = BOARD_PX / 2 + white_cp * (BOARD_PX / 2 - 8) / lim;
    if (s->flipped) {
        samGL_HardwareDrawRect(EVAL_X, BOARD_Y, EVAL_W, white_px, COL_WHITE);
        samGL_HardwareDrawRect(EVAL_X, BOARD_Y + white_px, EVAL_W, BOARD_PX - white_px, COL_BLACK);
    } else {
        samGL_HardwareDrawRect(EVAL_X, BOARD_Y, EVAL_W, BOARD_PX - white_px, COL_BLACK);
        samGL_HardwareDrawRect(EVAL_X, BOARD_Y + BOARD_PX - white_px, EVAL_W, white_px, COL_WHITE);
    }
    samGL_Flush();
}

/* Thinking bar: empty it, then fill it from the bottom as time passes.
 * Only the newly filled rows are drawn, so calling it often is cheap. */
static void render_think_clear(Screen *s) {
    samGL_HardwareDrawRect(SIDE_X, THINK_Y, THINK_W, THINK_H, COL_FRAME);
    s->think_rows = 0;
}

static void render_think(Screen *s, u32 elapsed_ms, u32 budget_ms) {
    int rows = (int)((uint64_t)THINK_H * elapsed_ms / budget_ms);
    if (rows > THINK_H) rows = THINK_H;
    if (rows > s->think_rows) {
        samGL_HardwareDrawRect(SIDE_X, THINK_Y + THINK_H - rows, THINK_W,
                               rows - s->think_rows, COL_THINK_BAR);
        s->think_rows = rows;
    }
}

/* Draw everything from scratch: after reset, "new" or "flip". */
static void render_all(Screen *s, const Position *p, Move last, int white_cp) {
    samGL_HardwareClearScreen(COL_BACKGROUND);
    samGL_HardwareDrawRect(BOARD_X - FRAME_PX, BOARD_Y - FRAME_PX,
                           BOARD_PX + 2 * FRAME_PX, BOARD_PX + 2 * FRAME_PX, COL_FRAME);
    samGL_HardwareDrawRect(EVAL_X - 1, BOARD_Y - 1, EVAL_W + 2, BOARD_PX + 2, COL_FRAME);
    memset(s->cell, CELL_UNKNOWN, sizeof s->cell);   /* forces a full redraw */
    render_board(s, p, last);
    render_eval(s, white_cp);
    render_think_clear(s);
}

#endif

The evaluation bar converts the engine's score to White's point of view, clamps it to ±800 centipawns (eight pawns: a decisive advantage), and splits the bar's 224 pixels. The thinking bar draws only the rows it has not drawn yet, so the main loop can call render_think every time round without flooding the bus.

Check

This frame comes from running main_game.c against models of your GPU and the UART and the real chess core in simulation, right after you play e2e4 and the engine answers b8c6. Only the last move is highlighted, the evaluation bar leans slightly to White (the engine scored −25 for itself), the lamp is green and the thinking bar has been emptied for your turn:

47The game loop

Goal: tie the UART, the rules, the renderer and the chess core together, in one loop that never blocks.

Concept

The core only finds moves. It has no memory of the game, so it cannot see a repeated position or the fifty-move rule, and it does not check your moves. The Cortex-A9 does that, with the same chess.h:

Create sw/game.h
/* game.h - the rules the hardware does not know: is the human's move legal,
 * and is the game over? Your game loop owns one Game (make it static: it
 * holds the position history). */
#ifndef GAME_H
#define GAME_H

#include "chess.h"

#define MAX_HISTORY 128

typedef enum {
    GAME_PLAYING, GAME_CHECKMATE, GAME_STALEMATE, GAME_REPETITION, GAME_FIFTY_MOVES
} GameState;

typedef struct {
    Position current;
    Position history[MAX_HISTORY];   /* positions since the last pawn move or capture */
    int      history_count;
    int      quiet_plies;            /* fifty-move counter, in plies */
} Game;

static inline void game_init(Game *g, const Position *start) {
    g->current = *start;
    g->history[0] = *start;
    g->history_count = 1;
    g->quiet_plies = 0;
}

/* 1 if move m is legal in the current position. */
static inline int game_is_legal(const Game *g, Move m) {
    Move list[MAX_MOVES];
    int n = generate_moves(&g->current, list, 0), i;
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (list[i] == m) {
            Position child = g->current;
            make_move(&child, m);
            return legal_after(&child, m);
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Play a move that is already known to be legal. */
static inline void game_play(Game *g, Move m) {
    int pawn_move = (g->current.bb[g->current.side * 6 + PAWN] & BIT(MOVE_FROM(m))) != 0;
    int capture   = (occupied(&g->current) & BIT(MOVE_TO(m))) != 0;
    make_move(&g->current, m);
    if (pawn_move || capture) {          /* no earlier position can repeat */
        g->history_count = 0;
        g->quiet_plies = 0;
    } else {
        g->quiet_plies++;
    }
    if (g->history_count < MAX_HISTORY) g->history[g->history_count++] = g->current;
}

static inline int same_position(const Position *a, const Position *b) {
    return memcmp(a->bb, b->bb, sizeof a->bb) == 0 && a->side == b->side
        && a->castle == b->castle && a->ep == b->ep;
}

static inline GameState game_state(const Game *g) {
    Move list[MAX_MOVES];
    int n = generate_moves(&g->current, list, 0), i, any_legal = 0, repeats = 0;
    for (i = 0; i < n && !any_legal; i++) {
        Position child = g->current;
        make_move(&child, list[i]);
        any_legal = legal_after(&child, list[i]);
    }
    if (!any_legal) return in_check(&g->current) ? GAME_CHECKMATE : GAME_STALEMATE;
    if (g->quiet_plies >= 100) return GAME_FIFTY_MOVES;
    for (i = 0; i < g->history_count; i++)
        if (same_position(&g->history[i], &g->current)) repeats++;
    return repeats >= 3 ? GAME_REPETITION : GAME_PLAYING;
}

#endif

Line by line

  1. Game holds the current position plus every position since the last pawn move or capture. Only those can ever repeat, because pawn moves and captures cannot be undone. quiet_plies counts towards the fifty-move rule (100 plies).
  2. game_is_legal checks a move from the human: it must appear in the generated list, and the mover's king must be safe afterwards. The same two tests the engine uses, so the human and the engine play by exactly the same rules.
  3. game_play makes the move. A pawn move or capture resets the history and the counter; then the new position is appended.
  4. game_state decides whether the game is over. No legal move: checkmate if in check, else stalemate. Then the fifty-move rule. Then repetition: the current position appearing three times in the history.
  5. same_position compares boards, side, rights and en-passant square: two positions are "the same" for repetition only if all of these match.

The game itself is a small state machine with three modes. Every change to the game goes through one function, next_turn, which redraws and then decides the next mode, so the screen can never fall out of step with the game.

Code

All state is static. Game holds up to 128 positions of history, about 14 KB, and the bare-metal stack is small. THINK_MS is the engine's time per move: 2 seconds gives depth 6 or 7 in the middle game.

Create sw/main_game.cpart 1 of 5
/* main_game.c - play chess on the PYNQ-Z2.
 * You type moves on a serial terminal. The Cortex-A9 checks them, draws the
 * board with samGL, and asks the chess core in the PL for its reply. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include "chess_pl.h"
#include "game.h"
#include "render.h"
#include "uart_in.h"

#ifndef THINK_MS
#define THINK_MS 2000            /* the engine's time per move        */
#endif
#define MAX_DEPTH      20        /* iterative deepening stops here     */
#define MAX_GAME_PLIES 512

static const char *START_FEN = "rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1";

typedef enum { WAIT_HUMAN, ENGINE_THINKING, GAME_OVER } Mode;

/* Everything lives in static variables: Game alone is about 14 KB. */
static Game       game;                  /* position + repetition history */
static Thinker    thinker;               /* the engine's search, in the PL */
static Screen     screen;                /* what the VGA screen shows      */
static LineReader line;                  /* the line being typed           */
static Position   start_pos;             /* for "undo", which replays      */
static Move       played[MAX_GAME_PLIES];
static int        played_count;
static Mode       mode;
static int        engine_side = BLACK;
static Move       last_move;
static int        eval_white;            /* engine's last score, White's view */

Parsing works in two steps: first the shape of the text, then the rules. Building the move from the text and asking game_is_legal means the parser needs no chess knowledge of its own: castling (e1g1) and en passant are just moves in the legal list. A pawn reaching the last rank without a letter becomes a queen, because that is nearly always what you want.

Add to sw/main_game.cpart 2 of 5
/* Turn "e2e4" or "e7e8q" into a legal Move, or 0. Castling is the king's
 * two-square move (e1g1). A promotion without a letter becomes a queen. */
static Move parse_move(const Game *g, const char *s) {
    int from, to, promo = 0;
    if (strlen(s) < 4 || strlen(s) > 5) return 0;
    if (s[0] < 'a' || s[0] > 'h' || s[1] < '1' || s[1] > '8') return 0;
    if (s[2] < 'a' || s[2] > 'h' || s[3] < '1' || s[3] > '8') return 0;
    from = (s[0] - 'a') + 8 * (s[1] - '1');
    to   = (s[2] - 'a') + 8 * (s[3] - '1');
    if (s[4]) {
        static const char LETTERS[] = "nbrq";            /* KNIGHT=1 ... QUEEN=4 */
        const char *p = strchr(LETTERS, s[4]);
        if (!p) return 0;
        promo = KNIGHT + (int)(p - LETTERS);
    } else if ((g->current.bb[g->current.side * 6 + PAWN] & BIT(from))
               && (to >> 3 == 0 || to >> 3 == 7)) {
        promo = QUEEN;
    }
    return game_is_legal(g, MAKE_MOVE(from, to, promo)) ? MAKE_MOVE(from, to, promo) : 0;
}

/* The board as text on the terminal: White in capitals, rank 8 on top. */
static void print_board(const Position *p) {
    static const char LETTER[] = "PNBRQKpnbrqk";
    int rank, file, i;
    for (rank = 7; rank >= 0; rank--) {
        printf("  %d ", rank + 1);
        for (file = 0; file < 8; file++) {
            char c = '.';
            for (i = 0; i < 12; i++)
                if (p->bb[i] & BIT(rank * 8 + file)) c = LETTER[i];
            printf(" %c", c);
        }
        printf("\r\n");
    }
    printf("     a b c d e f g h\r\n");
}

static void print_help(void) {
    printf("Type a move like e2e4 (castle: e1g1, promote: e7e8q), or:\r\n"
           "  new    start again        undo   take back your last move\r\n"
           "  go     engine plays now   stop   engine moves at once\r\n"
           "  flip   turn the board     board  print the board here\r\n"
           "  fen <FEN>  set up a position\r\n");
}

undo does not try to reverse moves. It replays the game from the start, minus the last moves, which is simple and keeps the repetition history exactly right. Replaying a few hundred moves takes well under a millisecond.

Add to sw/main_game.cpart 3 of 5
static void play(Move m) {
    game_play(&game, m);
    played[played_count++] = m;
    last_move = m;
}

static void start_thinking(void) {
    mode = ENGINE_THINKING;
    render_lamp(COL_THINKING);
    render_think_clear(&screen);
    think_begin(&thinker, &game.current, MAX_DEPTH, THINK_MS);
}

/* Called after every change to the game: redraw, then decide who moves. */
static void next_turn(void) {
    static const char *const RESULT[] = { "", "checkmate", "stalemate, a draw",
        "threefold repetition, a draw", "fifty-move rule, a draw" };
    GameState st = game_state(&game);

    render_board(&screen, &game.current, last_move);
    if (st != GAME_PLAYING) {
        mode = GAME_OVER;
        render_lamp(COL_GAME_OVER);
        printf("Game over: %s", RESULT[st]);
        if (st == GAME_CHECKMATE) printf(", %s wins", game.current.side == WHITE ? "Black" : "White");
        printf(". Type new to play again.\r\n");
    } else if (game.current.side == engine_side) {
        start_thinking();
    } else {
        mode = WAIT_HUMAN;
        render_lamp(COL_YOUR_TURN);
        render_think_clear(&screen);
        printf("%s to move> ", game.current.side == WHITE ? "White" : "Black");
        fflush(stdout);                    /* show the prompt before Enter */
    }
}

static void new_game(const Position *p) {
    start_pos = *p;
    game_init(&game, p);
    played_count = 0;
    last_move = 0;
    eval_white = 0;
    render_all(&screen, &game.current, last_move, eval_white);
    next_turn();
}

/* Take back moves by replaying the game from the start, so the repetition
 * history stays exactly right. Undo stops on the human's turn. */
static void undo(void) {
    int n = played_count, i;
    if (n == 0) { printf("Nothing to undo.\r\n"); return; }
    do {
        n--;
        game_init(&game, &start_pos);
        for (i = 0; i < n; i++) game_play(&game, played[i]);
    } while (n > 0 && game.current.side == engine_side);
    played_count = n;
    last_move = n ? played[n - 1] : 0;
    next_turn();
}

static void engine_moved(const PlResult *r) {
    char text[6];
    int mate = r->score >= MATE - MAX_PLY || r->score <= -MATE + MAX_PLY;
    uint64_t ms = (uint64_t)(r->cycles / 50000);           /* 50 MHz core */

    move_to_text(r->best, text);
    eval_white = game.current.side == WHITE ? r->score : -r->score;
    printf("Engine plays %s  (depth %d, %s %d, %llu nodes, %llu knodes/s)\r\n",
           text, r->depth, mate ? "mate score" : "score", r->score,
           (unsigned long long)r->nodes,
           (unsigned long long)(ms ? r->nodes / ms : 0));
    play(r->best);
    render_eval(&screen, eval_white);
    next_turn();
}

Line by line

  1. play is the only place a move is made: it updates the rules (game_play), the move list used by undo, and last_move for the highlight.
  2. start_thinking turns the lamp red, empties the thinking bar, and hands the position to the PL with think_begin. It returns immediately; the search runs in hardware.
  3. next_turn is the heart of the program. It redraws (only the changed squares), then picks the next mode: game over (yellow lamp and a message), the engine's turn (start thinking), or yours (green lamp and the prompt). Every action ends by calling it, so the screen and the mode can never disagree.
  4. new_game stores the starting position (needed by undo), resets the history, draws everything from scratch, and calls next_turn.
  5. undo replays the game from the start without the last move, and repeats while it is still the engine's turn, so you always land on your own move.
  6. engine_moved prints the move with its depth, score and speed, turns the score into White's point of view for the evaluation bar, plays the move, and calls next_turn.

engine_moved reports the speed in thousands of nodes per second, computed from the core's own clock counter: on a 50 MHz core, cycles / 50000 is milliseconds. The score is printed from the engine's side; the evaluation bar converts it to White's.

Add to sw/main_game.cpart 4 of 5
static void handle_line(const char *s) {
    Position p;
    Move m;

    if (mode == ENGINE_THINKING) {                 /* only "stop" while thinking */
        if (strcmp(s, "stop") == 0) pl_abort();
        else printf("The engine is thinking; type stop to make it move now.\r\n");
        return;
    }
    if (strcmp(s, "help") == 0)        { print_help(); next_turn(); }
    else if (strcmp(s, "new") == 0)    { from_fen(START_FEN, &p); engine_side = BLACK; new_game(&p); }
    else if (strcmp(s, "undo") == 0)   undo();
    else if (strcmp(s, "board") == 0)  { print_board(&game.current); next_turn(); }
    else if (strcmp(s, "flip") == 0) {
        screen.flipped = !screen.flipped;
        render_all(&screen, &game.current, last_move, eval_white);
        next_turn();
    }
    else if (strcmp(s, "go") == 0 && mode == WAIT_HUMAN) {
        engine_side = game.current.side;           /* swap sides with the engine */
        start_thinking();
    }
    else if (strncmp(s, "fen ", 4) == 0) {
        if (from_fen(s + 4, &p)) new_game(&p);
        else { printf("Could not read that FEN.\r\n"); next_turn(); }
    }
    else if (mode == GAME_OVER) printf("Game over. Type new or undo.\r\n");
    else if ((m = parse_move(&game, s)) != 0) { play(m); next_turn(); }
    else { printf("Not a legal move: %s (type help)\r\n", s); next_turn(); }
}

Line by line

  1. While the engine thinks, only stop does something: it writes ABORT to the core. Everything else gets a short message, so a stray key can never corrupt the game.
  2. Each command is a plain strcmp. After any command that changes nothing on the board, next_turn reprints the prompt.
  3. flip toggles the view and redraws everything, because every square moves on screen.
  4. go swaps sides with the engine: it now plays the side to move, and starts thinking at once.
  5. Anything else is tried as a move. parse_move returns 0 for text that is not a legal move here, and the message tells you so.

While the engine thinks, only stop is accepted. It sends ABORT; the thinker then returns the move from the last depth that finished, so even a stopped search plays a sensible move.

Add to sw/main_game.cpart 5 of 5
int main(void) {
    Position p;

    samGL_Init();
    if (!pl_present()) {
        printf("Chess core not found: ID register reads %08lx\r\n", (unsigned long)pl_read(REG_ID));
        return 1;
    }
    printf("\r\nFPGA chess. You are White.\r\n");
    print_help();
    from_fen(START_FEN, &p);
    new_game(&p);

    for (;;) {
        if (uart_poll_line(&line)) handle_line(line.text);

        if (mode == ENGINE_THINKING) {
            PlResult r;
            if (think_poll(&thinker, &r)) {
                engine_moved(&r);
            } else {
                XTime now;
                XTime_GetTime(&now);
                render_think(&screen, (u32)((now - thinker.t0) * 1000 / COUNTS_PER_SECOND), THINK_MS);
            }
        }
        /* anything else your game animates goes here: the loop never blocks */
    }
}

Line by line

  1. samGL_Init prints your GPU's version. pl_present checks the chess core answers with the right ID; if not, there is no point going on, so the program says why and stops.
  2. The help text, then new_game with the standard start: the screen is drawn and the first prompt appears.
  3. The endless loop polls the UART for a finished line, and, while the engine thinks, polls the core. If the core is not finished yet, it updates the thinking bar from the elapsed time: (now - t0) * 1000 / COUNTS_PER_SECOND converts timer ticks to milliseconds.

The loop body is two polls. Neither ever waits, so the loop also has room for anything else your game animates, such as a clock.

48Build, run, and play

Goal: a game of chess on the monitor, with your moves typed on the PC.

  1. Set the PYNQ-Z2's boot jumper to JTAG. Connect the monitor to the VGA output, the micro-USB cable to PROG/UART, and switch on.
  2. Find the COM port: Windows Device Manager, Ports (COM & LPT). The board shows up as a USB serial port.
  3. Open PuTTY. Connection type: Serial, your COM port, speed 115200. Under Connection, Serial: 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, no parity, flow control None. Under Terminal, set Local echo and Local line editing to Force off: the board echoes for you. Open.
  4. In Vitis, build chess_game, then Run (Classic: Run As, Launch Hardware) with Program FPGA and Run ps7_init enabled.
  5. Click into PuTTY and type your moves.

Part 5

Making it stronger

Add upgrades one at a time, only after Part 3 works. The rule never changes: change the C first, regenerate the vectors, then make the RTL match.

49Killer moves: a tested upgrade

Goal: better move ordering, so alpha-beta cuts off sooner, with exactly the same answers.

Concept

Remember Step 14: alpha-beta is only as fast as its move ordering. Our generator already puts captures first, but quiet moves come out in board order. The killer heuristic improves that with one observation: a quiet move that refuted one position often refutes its siblings too. If ...Qh4 punished one White move, it probably punishes a similar one.

So for each ply, remember the last quiet move that caused a cutoff (the "killer"), and at the next node on that ply, try it first among the quiet moves. It is an ordering change only, so the search's score and best move can't change, only the amount of work. Measured at depth 6:

PositionNodes beforeNodes with killersScore and move
Start1,519,394159,788unchanged
Kiwipete2,312,7152,197,846unchanged
pos61,864,1961,408,694unchanged

The gain ranges from 5% to almost 90%, and it is largest in quiet positions, where the captures-first rule has nothing to work with. On the board, the depth-6 search from the start drops from 56 million clocks to 7.1 million, and the one-second think reaches depth 7 instead of 5.

How the hardware does it. The generator already writes quiet moves one by one. When it is about to write the killer, it writes the first quiet move in the killer's place instead, then spends one extra clock writing the killer into the first quiet slot. The two trade places, and the C does exactly the same swap, so the lists still match move for move.

This upgrade was fully tested: the C killer engine passes perft, and the hardware matched it on all 577 full-set searches. The finished files are in the ZIP, under upgrades/killer/.

Code

Apply these changes in order. Each "find" text appears exactly once in its file.

/* A quiet move: no promotion, nothing captured (en passant is a capture). */
static inline int is_quiet(const Position *p, Move m) {
    int pawn = (p->bb[p->side * 6 + PAWN] & BIT(MOVE_FROM(m))) != 0;
    if (MOVE_PROMO(m)) return 0;
    if (occupied(p) & BIT(MOVE_TO(m))) return 0;
    if (pawn && (MOVE_FROM(m) & 7) != (MOVE_TO(m) & 7)) return 0;
    return 1;
}

          end
        end

        G_TARGETS: begin
Replace with
          end else if (stage == last_stage) begin
            if (captures_only) first_quiet <= count;
            done <= 1'b1;
            state <= G_IDLE;
          end else begin
            stage <= stage + 3'd1;
            state <= G_STAGE;
          end
        end

        G_TARGETS: begin

Change 12 in rtl/move_gen.sv. Remember the first quiet move, and start the swap.

Find
            if (count == 8'hFF) overflow <= 1'b1;
            count <= count + 8'd1;
            if (is_promo && promo != 3'd1) begin
Replace with
            if (count == 8'hFF) overflow <= 1'b1;
            count <= count + 8'd1;
            if (count == first_quiet) first_quiet_move <= new_move;
            if (swap_now) state <= G_SWAP;
            if (is_promo && promo != 3'd1) begin

Change 13 in rtl/move_gen.sv. Add the new state.

Find
        default: state <= G_IDLE;
      endcase
Replace with
        G_SWAP: state <= G_EMIT;             // the killer is written during this clock

        default: state <= G_IDLE;
      endcase

Change 14 in rtl/search_core.sv. Add a state.

Find
    S_NEXT, S_READ, S_DECODE, S_APPLY, S_TEST, S_LEGAL, S_END_NODE, S_RETURN, S_POP, S_SCORE
Replace with
    S_NEXT, S_READ, S_DECODE, S_APPLY, S_TEST, S_LEGAL, S_END_NODE, S_RETURN, S_POP, S_SCORE,
    S_KILLER

Change 15 in rtl/search_core.sv. That makes 17 states, which no longer fit in four bits.

Find
  typedef enum logic [3:0] {
Replace with
  typedef enum logic [4:0] {

Change 16 in rtl/search_core.sv. The frame must remember where the quiet moves begin.

Find
    logic [7:0]         count;       // moves in this node's list
Replace with
    logic [7:0]         count;       // moves in this node's list
    logic [7:0]         first_quiet; // index of this node's first quiet move

Change 17 in rtl/search_core.sv. Killer storage: a small RAM, plus valid bits that clear in one clock.

Find
  logic  [7:0]  gen_count;
Replace with
  logic  [7:0]  gen_count, gen_first_quiet;
  move_t        killer [0:MAX_PLY-1];
  logic [MAX_PLY-1:0] killer_valid;
  move_t        killer_r;

Change 18 in rtl/search_core.sv. Connect the generator.

Find
    .clk, .rst, .start(gen_start), .pos, .captures_only(stand_pat), .ply,
    .done(gen_done), .count(gen_count), .overflow(gen_overflow),
Replace with
    .clk, .rst, .start(gen_start), .pos, .captures_only(stand_pat), .ply,
    .killer(killer_r), .first_quiet(gen_first_quiet),
    .done(gen_done), .count(gen_count), .overflow(gen_overflow),

Change 19 in rtl/search_core.sv. Initialize at the start of a search.

Find
                 depth: depth, index: 8'd0, count: 8'd0,
                 any_legal: 1'b0, in_check: 1'b0};
Replace with
                 depth: depth, index: 8'd0, count: 8'd0, first_quiet: 8'd0,
                 any_legal: 1'b0, in_check: 1'b0};
          killer_valid <= '0;

Change 20 in rtl/search_core.sv. Hand this ply's killer to the generator.

Find
        S_GEN_START: begin
          gen_start <= 1'b1;
Replace with
        S_GEN_START: begin
          killer_r <= killer_valid[ply] ? killer[ply] : '0;
          gen_start <= 1'b1;

Change 21 in rtl/search_core.sv. Store the quiet start in the frame.

Find
          f.count <= gen_count;
Replace with
          f.count <= gen_count;
          f.first_quiet <= gen_first_quiet;

Change 22 in rtl/search_core.sv. Initialize the child frame.

Find
                   index: 8'd0, count: 8'd0, any_legal: 1'b0, in_check: 1'b0};
Replace with
                   index: 8'd0, count: 8'd0, first_quiet: 8'd0,
                   any_legal: 1'b0, in_check: 1'b0};

Change 23 in rtl/search_core.sv. On a quiet cutoff, go and read the move that caused it.

Find
            ret <= new_best;           // beta cutoff
            state <= S_RETURN;
          end else begin
Replace with
            ret <= new_best;           // beta cutoff
            // The move RAM is already addressed with {ply, f.index}; its output
            // is the move that caused this cutoff, one clock from now.
            state <= (f.index >= f.first_quiet) ? S_KILLER : S_RETURN;
          end else begin

Change 24 in rtl/search_core.sv. Store it.

Find
        default: state <= S_IDLE;
      endcase
    end
  end
endmodule
Replace with
        S_KILLER: begin
          killer[ply] <= move_rdata;
          killer_valid[ply] <= 1'b1;
          state <= S_RETURN;
        end

        default: state <= S_IDLE;
      endcase
    end
  end
endmodule

Change 25 in tb/tb_move_gen.sv. The generator testbench needs the two new ports. With no killer the list order is unchanged.

Find
  move_gen dut (.clk, .rst, .start, .pos, .captures_only, .ply(5'd3),
Replace with
  move_gen dut (.clk, .rst, .start, .pos, .captures_only, .ply(5'd3),
                .killer('0), .first_quiet(),
Check
Command Prompt
cd /d C:\chess\c
gcc -std=c99 -O2 -Wall -Wextra main.c -o engine.exe
engine.exe test
gcc -std=c99 -O2 -Wall -Wextra gen_vectors.c -o gen_vectors.exe
gen_vectors.exe ..\vectors
cd ..
scripts\run_sim.bat tb_move_gen
scripts\run_sim.bat tb_search
scripts\run_sim.bat tb_axi

All must pass. The estimated size stays about the same (11,478 LUTs, 16 block RAMs). Perft counts and their clock counts don't change, because perft never records a killer.

50What to add next

These are not built or tested here. They are the directions I would take, roughly in order of value for effort. Note which kind each is, because it decides how you test it:

KindExamplesHow to test
Ordering onlykillers, history, hash movescore at each depth must not change; nodes should fall
Window onlyaspiration windows, PVSscore must not change; re-searches may add work
Selectivenull move, late-move reductionsscore can change: judge by test suites and by playing games
UpgradeWhat it doesHardware notes
Previous best move firstat the root, search last iteration's best move firstone register; makes iterative deepening really pay off
Second killercatches more quiet refutationsa second killer table and swap
Zobrist hashinga 64-bit fingerprint for each positiona ROM of 781 random constants, updated with XOR on each move
Repetition in searchstops walking into drawsneeds the hash; compare against the path and the game history from the CPU
Transposition tablereuses results for positions reached by different move orders8,192 entries is about 24 block RAMs; store key, score, depth, bound and move
Null move pruningif passing still beats β, cut offflip side, clear en passant, reduce depth; never in check, nor with only pawns left
Better evaluationmobility, passed pawns, king safetyside_attacks already exists; add a stage to eval_pipe

For speed, measure before changing anything. The cycles and nodes counters are always there; add counters for generator-busy and evaluator-wait clocks, and fix whichever is largest.

Troubleshooting

C and simulation

SymptomCheck
A perft count is wrongdivide at the shallowest failing depth (Step 9)
xvlog is not recognisedrun settings64.bat in this window
xvlog can't find a file in rtl\create the placeholders from Step 23
cannot open vec_...txtrun gen_vectors.exe ..\vectors
A simulation never endsa testbench is waiting on done: add -debug typical and look at state
A simulation is very slownormal for xsim: use the quick vectors and let it run

Vivado

SymptomCheck
Add Module doesn't list chess_axi_topall seven files in Design Sources; it must be the .v file; try Tools, Refresh Hierarchy
Error about a SystemVerilog module referenceyou referenced chess_axi, not chess_axi_top
The block shows dozens of separate s_axi_ pinsthe bus wasn't recognised: right-click the block, Refresh Module, and check the port names
The core shows as unassigned in the Address Editorright-click, Assign; check again after any Refresh Module
chess_pkg is not declaredcompile order: chess_pkg.sv first, type SystemVerilog
0 block RAMsread the sdp_ram messages in the synthesis log
Negative WNSStep 37. Never ship with it
Critical warning about DDR or FIXED_IORun Block Automation with Apply Board Preset

On the board

SymptomCheck
The CPU freezes reading the IDthe logic isn't programmed or its clock is stopped: a read with nobody answering hangs the bus. Check Program FPGA, or that Overlay ran first
ID reads zero or garbagewrong address: compare with the Address Editor
Overlay error about .hwhthe .bit and .hwh names differ, or the file is missing
Perft wrong on the board, right in simulationtiming first: read WNS. Then clock and reset
Clock counts differ, nodes matchyou changed the RTL (expected after a timing fix) or added an upgrade
FAULT bit seta move list overflowed: an impossible position. Check the FEN
Best move is 0mate or stalemate: check with game_state
Results look randomthe order of the board writes: low word, then high word, for each board
64-bit numbers print wronglythe C library in your BSP may lack %llu: print the high and low 32-bit halves instead
Nothing on the serial portCOM port and 115200 baud, and the board in JTAG boot mode

To read a register without any of your code, use the XSCT console in Vitis, once the processor is initialised and the logic is programmed. It should print C4E55A01:

Tcl console
connect
targets -set -filter {name =~ "*A9*#0"}
mrd 0x43C00000

Final checklist

Rules
  • engine.exe test passes all 30 counts
  • tb_functions and tb_move_gen pass
  • board perft matches, clock counts included
Search
  • tb_search passes
  • the board's depth 1 to 6 table matches
  • mate, stalemate and promotion tests pass
  • an aborted search never changes the move
Implementation
  • WNS and WHS both zero or more
  • no latches or multi-driven nets
  • about 16 block RAMs inferred
  • your VGA design still meets timing
Game
  • human moves checked by game_is_legal
  • the screen keeps drawing while the engine thinks
  • checkmate, stalemate, repetition and the fifty-move rule end the game

References

  1. C. Donninger, A. Kure and U. Lorenz, Parallel Brutus: The First Distributed, FPGA Accelerated Chess Program, IPDPS 2004. The inspiration for the hardware architecture; this design is new, not the Brutus source.
  2. D. E. Knuth and R. W. Moore, An Analysis of Alpha-Beta Pruning, Artificial Intelligence, 1975.
  3. C. E. Shannon, Programming a Computer for Playing Chess, 1950.
  4. FIDE Laws of Chess: movement, castling, en passant, promotion and draws.
  5. Chess Programming Wiki: Perft Results and Simplified Evaluation Function.
  6. AMD, Zynq-7000 SoC Technical Reference Manual (UG585).
  7. AMD, Vivado Synthesis (UG901): HDL coding styles and RAM inference.
  8. AMD, Limitations of the Module Reference Feature (UG994).
  9. AMD, Zynq-7000 Embedded Design Tutorial (UG1165).
  10. PYNQ: Overlay design, PYNQ-Z2 setup, Jupyter notebooks, and the forum tutorial Creating a hardware design for PYNQ.
  11. TUL, PYNQ-Z2 product page.

Every code snippet on this page was extracted from this HTML file into an empty folder, rebuilt and re-tested before delivery: C with gcc and clang, the RTL with Verilator against the C engine's vectors, and the drivers against the simulated hardware. Vivado, Vitis and the physical board were not available, so Part 3 is untested.
